#6017. Dakota Meyer survived a battle he thought would kill him. 15 years after leaving the Marines, he went back

Dakota Meyer opens up about the battle that changed his life, his difficult transition home and the decision to reenlist in his late 30s.

Fifteen years after Dakota Meyer left the Marine Corps, the Medal of Honor recipient decided to put the uniform back on — becoming the first with the award to ever reenlist.

Meyer was 36. He had fought in Afghanistan, struggled with the transition home from war and spent years building a life outside the military. But he said the desire to serve never went away.

"Every day after I took that uniform off, that desire to serve didn't just end because my commitment to the country did," Meyer told Fox News Digital in an interview ahead of Veterans Day.

AMERICAN WAR HERO DETAILS DIRE LIVING CONDITIONS US TROOPS FACE AS HEGSETH TAPS HIM TO 'FIX' IT

Meyer rejects the idea that receiving the Medal of Honor meant he had already done enough.

"I think sometimes it's looked at as you've done your part, and I am wholeheartedly against that," he said. "I believe that the only time you've done your part is when you've done all that you can."

Medal of Honor recipient Dakota Meyer speaks with a young girl while wearing the nation’s highest military decoration. (Courtesy of Dakota Meyer)

For Meyer, Veterans Day is a reminder that service does not necessarily end when someone leaves the military.

"Sometimes we look at the veteran title as it is something that represents something we've done," Meyer said. "And it's not. It's something that we are doing, and it is something that we can continue to do."

Meyer reenlisted in 2025 and later entered the training pipeline to become a reconnaissance Marine, completing the grueling course in his late 30s.

"To be able to do that at 38, it was definitely one of the — hands down — probably the hardest thing that I've ever had to do," Meyer said.

His first stint in the Marines had taken him to Afghanistan, where at 21 he fought in the 2009 Battle of Ganjgal in Kunar Province.

Meyer had been assigned to remain with the vehicles at a rally point while other members of his team accompanied Afghan troops toward the village roughly a mile away. The patrol was ambushed by more than 50 insurgents firing from fortified positions on the surrounding slopes.

War Secretary Pete Hegseth administers the oath of enlistment to Medal of Honor recipient Dakota Meyer as Meyer returns to the Marine Corps after 15 years out of uniform. (Courtesy of Dakota Meyer)

MEDAL OF HONOR RECIPIENT JAMES CAPERS JR. SAYS RECOGNITION IS BITTERSWEET AFTER LOSING 'SO MUCH'

Meyer and Staff Sgt. Juan Rodriguez-Chavez could hear the battle unfolding over the radio. Four members of Meyer's team were trapped inside the ambush.

After repeatedly asking for permission to go in, Meyer and Rodriguez-Chavez drove toward the fighting, with Meyer manning the gun turret.

"I think often we try to make these decisions as if it's some heroic decision, and it's really not," Meyer said. "It's just about following through on what my promise that I had made to them."

The pair made repeated trips into the ambush, helping evacuate wounded troops as Meyer continued searching for his teammates.

"I think it was at that point that I did realize that I just accepted that I was going to die," Meyer recalled. "But I was gonna make sure that I would do everything I could up until that last breath."

His four teammates were ultimately found dead. Meyer would receive the Medal of Honor for his actions that day.

Leaving the Marines the following year brought a different battle.

"I struggled. I mean, I struggled," Meyer said. "The horrors of war definitely haunted me when I got out."

Dakota Meyer, second from right, relaxes with fellow service members while deployed to Afghanistan. Meyer was 21 when he fought in the 2009 Battle of Ganjgal. (Courtesy of Dakota Meyer)

Meyer said one of the hardest parts of returning to civilian life was figuring out what could replace the sense of purpose he had found in the military.

"The hardest part was finding purpose," he said. "It wasn't about being successful in anything."

Eventually, he said, he realized that neither money nor professional success was what he was looking for. He wanted to feel that his work had an impact.

Years later, while speaking to a group of Marines at Camp Pendleton, that question of purpose came back to him in a different way.

A Marine attending a leadership course told Meyer he was deciding whether to reenlist. He had a family and could make more money outside the military, but he loved serving.

"Do you think it's still worth serving?" he asked.

Meyer said yes, but the answer bothered him.

"I felt it was one of the most unbecoming things that I had ever said back to that crowd," Meyer said, explaining that he was telling someone else to accept the sacrifices of continued service while he was free to return to civilian life.

"I told them that I would walk out of there and I would go about reenlisting, or I would never say that to anybody again."

It ultimately took Meyer about two years to return to the Marines.

Dakota Meyer, right, sits with fellow members of his team while deployed to Afghanistan. Meyer later received the Medal of Honor for his actions during the Battle of Ganjgal. (Courtesy of Dakota Meyer)

Once back, he pursued a goal he had held since first seeing a Recon Marine poster in a recruiting office as a young man.

"They were the people that we were all trying to be inside of the Marine Corps," Meyer said.

At 37 and 38, keeping up physically wasn't necessarily the problem, but recovering felt different.

"What got me was the cumulative fatigue at my age," Meyer said. "These kids can recover like nothing else."

The experience also gave Meyer a close look at a generation of Marines nearly two decades younger than the one he had served alongside in Afghanistan.

"When we talk about service members or this next generation being weaker, it's absolutely not the case," Meyer said. "These kids are hands down, they will rise to the level of expectation that is set for them."

Meyer said the Marine Corps itself has changed since he left in 2010, but he viewed much of that change as necessary. He recalled younger Marines giving him an hour-long lesson on their "new language" during a break in training and said he often found himself learning from them.

"They do things a lot smarter," Meyer said. "I found myself learning a lot more from them than I did them probably learning from me."

He said today's young service members don't have a "generational problem," and said they still want the challenge, purpose and sense of belonging that drew those to serve before them.

#6016. Sexual harassment overhaul at a crossroads in the House

The leaders of an effort to overhaul how the House deals with sexual misconduct hope their proposal will see action before the end of the 119th Congress, though they’re split on the odds.

Rep. Kat Cammack, R-Fla., chair of the Republican Women’s Caucus, said legislative text is done and is being looked at by the relevant committees.

“Yes, absolutely,” she said when asked if the package would get a vote this year. “We’re shopping it now with the different committees, House Admin and Ethics, and waiting on their final feedback, which we should have actually this week.”

Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus, said she was still optimistic about getting it done, but stopped short of putting full faith in Republican leadership to get it over the finish line. The effort has been underway since May, when Cammack and Leger Fernández’s caucuses announced a partnership to propose changes after two members of the House resigned amid allegations of sexual misconduct.

Asked if she thought Speaker Mike Johnson would put the proposal on the floor during the busy lame-duck session, Leger Fernández laughed.

“Hopefully, that’s something that will happen, because you know the Republican Women’s Caucus had said they were optimistic before we left. I’m still optimistic,” she said.

The two groups have spent months holding dozens of meetings with staff, their own caucuses and male members of Congress, among others. Suggestions have included banning members of Congress from engaging in sexual relationships with any House staffer, not just those who work for them directly, and outlining penalties for violaters. Initially, the groups were expected to unveil their work by August recess, but that got pushed back as the House canceled weeks in session and as they cited a desire to get it right.

Cammack said she thinks Johnson “has been very sincere in his efforts on this.”

“That would be a tremendous disappointment” if he didn’t put it on the floor, she said when asked about the possibility. “I genuinely believe he cares about this issue.”

Leger Fernández said if it doesn’t get done by the end of the 119th Congress, she hopes some changes would be adopted under the rules package for the next Congress that Democrats bring forward in January. Such packages are typically adopted with party-line votes and give incoming majorities the chance to tweak how the House operates to their liking. While certain narrower proposals aimed at curbing sexual harassment could be written into House rules, others would need to pass both chambers and be enacted into law to take effect.

“We are going to move to make sure it is in the rules package, because we will be in charge next year,” Leger Fernández said. “But I would love for it to pass now, because that was a commitment that it be bipartisan.”

With the midterm elections over, the future of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth hangs in the balance. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is set to be speaker of the house, announced this weekend that he would vote in favor of a resolution to impeach Hegseth. The Defense Secretary is one of the most controversial figures in President Donald Trump’s cabinet, and has purged the Pentagon of many top officials widely perceived as highly effective. He has repeatedly made provocative culture-war comments that have little to do with national security. And most damaging to his reputation, Hegseth has become the face of the war in Iran.

No matter how unpopular the U.S. military operations have been, Hegseth has stood behind the president. He has defended the pledge to eliminate Iran’s nuclear program and to establish a stronger foothold in the region, even as voters, including those in red states, flocked to the polls to express their disapproval of the administration’s foreign policy.

With the midterm elections over, the future of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth hangs in the balance. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is set to be speaker of the house, announced this weekend that he would vote in favor of a resolution to impeach Hegseth. The Defense Secretary is one of the most controversial figures in President Donald Trump’s cabinet, and has purged the Pentagon of many top officials widely perceived as highly effective. He has repeatedly made provocative culture-war comments that have little to do with national security. And most damaging to his reputation, Hegseth has become the face of the war in Iran.

No matter how unpopular the U.S. military operations have been, Hegseth has stood behind the president. He has defended the pledge to eliminate Iran’s nuclear program and to establish a stronger foothold in the region, even as voters, including those in red states, flocked to the polls to express their disapproval of the administration’s foreign policy.

What happens next remains to be seen. Some Republicans privately hope Hegseth will resign, either voluntarily or under pressure, so that Trump can replace him with someone who has a more favorable public presence and clearer strategy for bringing U.S. involvement in the war to an end. Most Democrats are wary about initiating impeachment proceedings against Trump, given that he has only two years left in office and has historically benefited politically when under attack. Hegseth, however, remains a possible target for impeachment. Pursuing him, potentially with some Republican support, would allow Democrats to demonstrate that they are serious about holding the administration accountable.

Twenty years ago, Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld lost his job after becoming the face of an unpopular war. The question now is whether Hegseth will meet the same fate.

When President George W. Bush announced his nomination of Rumsfeld to be secretary of defense on Dec. 28, 2000, following a highly divisive election recount, most experts considered Rumsfeld one of the most qualified people for the job. A Navy veteran of the 1950s, he had served in the U.S. House of Representatives from 1963 to 1969. He then left legislative politics to become President Richard Nixon’s director of the Office of Economic Opportunity, and later counselor to the president and director of the Cost of Living Council. In 1973, Nixon named him U.S. ambassador to NATO. After Nixon resigned in disgrace over the Watergate scandal in August 1974, President Gerald Ford appointed Rumsfeld as White House chief of staff, and in 1975, Ford nominated him as secretary of defense, a post he held until President Jimmy Carter took office in 1977. Rumsfeld then spent many years working in the private sector while remaining involved in politics as a champion of neoconservatism.

His nomination as was greeted as a sign that the new President Bush would surround himself with a team of seasoned experts. After 9/11, Rumsfeld, who had a close and long-standing relationship with Vice President Dick Cheney, emerged as an important voice within the administration, helping to develop and implement a counterterrorism strategy intended to prevent comparable attacks on U.S. soil. In October and November 2001, the success of the military operations against the Taliban regime in Afghanistan was praised as evidence of his strategic prowess. The same was true in 2003, when the United States went to war with Iraq and Baghdad fell within weeks. On May 1, Bush declared an end to major combat operations beneath a “Mission Accomplished” banner, and in December, U.S. forces captured Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein.

Beneath those successes, however, things were already going wrong for Rumsfeld and for the war. The first major trouble came when looting broke out across Baghdad in April 2003, including at the Iraq Museum and the National Library and Archives. It soon became clear that the Pentagon had done little planning for the aftermath of Hussein’s downfall. “Stuff happens,” Rumsfeld told reporters, brushing off their questions about the looting. Meanwhile, the U.S. military failed to find stockpiles of weapons of mass destruction, which had been the main justification for the war.

By the 2006 midterms, the Iraq War was deeply unpopular. Large numbers of U.S. ground troops were still struggling to establish political stability and contain sectarian violence, and they were suffering heavy casualties. The 2003 decision to disband the Iraqi army proved enormously costly, and in April 2004, a weeknight 60 Minutes broadcast had revealed widespread abuse of detainees of Abu Ghraib prison. Although the story was initially framed as the work of a few rogue soldiers, it soon became clear that the abuses were connected to Pentagon policies authorizing harsh interrogation methods. Rumsfeld privately offered to resign several times, but Bush refused to accept.

There had also been scattered calls from Congress to force the issue. In May 2004, New York Rep. Charles Rangel introduced eight articles of impeachment against Rumsfeld in response to the revelations of Abu Ghraib.

After their tours of duty, many soldiers returned with post-traumatic stress disorder and could not get the support they needed to transition back to civilian life. Democrats made the war a central theme of the 2006 campaign, presenting it as evidence of Republican misrule: Bush’s deeply flawed and unnecessary decision to go to war with Iraq in the first place, made with strong congressional Republican support, compounded by the failure to plan for what would happen once the government collapsed. In September 2006, Republicans were able to block a vote on a nonbinding statement from Senate Democrats expressing a “sense of the Senate” that Bush replace Rumsfeld. “To fight a war on terror,” New York Sen. Charles Schumer said during the floor debate, “you need to be both strong and smart. And with Secretary Rumsfeld in this administration, you do see a great deal of strength but you don’t see enough on the smarts.” Behind the scenes, White House chief of staff Andrew Card lobbied the president, unsuccessfully, to replace Rumsfeld, too.

Rumsfeld himself was an issue. His approval ratings, which had stood at 71 percent in 2003, had fallen to 44 percent in Gallup polling by January 2006. That spring, in what Time called “The Revolt of the Generals,” six retired generals called for Rumsfeld to resign. “When I introduce the Secretary of Defense to my troops, I’m going to be a loyal subordinate,” Army Major General John Batiste told the magazine. “But it was boiling inside me. Every time I looked at him, I was thinking about … that s___ war plan, I was thinking about Abu Ghraib, and I was thinking about the challenges I had every day trying to rebuild the Iraqi military that he disbanded.”

Still, Bush stood by his man. Responding to critical editorials and calls for Rumsfeld’s resignation, Bush told the press on April 18: “Don Rumsfeld is doing a fine job. He’s not only transforming the military, he’s fighting a war on terror. … I hear the voices, and I read the front page, and I know the speculation. But I’m the decider, and I decide what’s best. And what’s best is for Don Rumsfeld to remain as the secretary of defense.” Whenever the issue came up in conversations with the White House, Robert Draper wrote in his 2007 book, Dead Certain, Bush doubled down. “The moment someone would say ‘Fire Donald Rumsfeld,’ Donald Rumsfeld would get a new lease on life,” said a White House aide.

The criticism did not abate. On Sept. 25, 2006, six weeks before the election, Batiste and two other retired generals told the Senate Democratic Policy Committee that Rumsfeld was unable to handle the job. On Saturday, Nov. 6, the newspapers associated with the Military Times Media Group published an editorial titled “Time for Rumsfeld to Go.”

Although Bush had publicly defended Rumsfeld into the final days of the campaign, the outcome made continued support all but impossible. A number of issues drove the election, including corruption, the cost of living, and healthcare, but opposition to the Iraq War was chief among them. Democrats won control of the House and Senate.

The president realized that he needed to change course. According to Rumsfeld, Cheney had given him advanced warning that Bush planned to finally accept his resignation. On Nov. 8, Bush announced that he was nominating Robert Gates as the new secretary of defense. “America is safer and the world is more secure because of the service and the leadership of Donald Rumsfeld,” Bush said. The decision was a blow to Cheney, who counted on Rumsfeld as an ally, and a victory for the foreign policy realists who served under President George H.W. Bush.

The leadership shake-up paved the way for a basic shift in strategy, announced in January 2007: from a U.S. mission focused on fighting insurgents and handing security over to newly constituted Iraqi forces, to a so-called surge of additional troops whose mission was to protect the Iraqi population and win their support against the insurgency.

Many Republicans privately expressed regret that Bush had not made the decision earlier, which might have given the GOP a fighting chance to hold its majorities. As New York Times reporter Adam Nagourney put it, then-Rep. Rahm Emanuel, an Illinois Democrat, “gave private thanks that the president had not robbed the Democrats of a potent issue by firing Rumsfeld before the campaign was engaged.”

The war in Iran is not nearly as large as the Iraq War, and there is no ground war, but Trump’s policies have proven to be extraordinarily unpopular from the start, and as prices rise, the war has only become more controversial. There is little love for Hegseth, even among Republicans. Not only does he embody much of what critics think is wrong with Trump 2.0, but because he is not the president, Republicans feel freer to attack him.

Rumsfeld’s resignation offers a template for today’s Republicans who are angry about what has happened in Trump’s second term, and it could be that Hegseth will now go. But even if he leaves—or if Congress forces him out—it is unlikely to bring a fundamental change in policy. The Trump White House has centralized power in the president himself, so he will remain the source of policy decisions and the focus of attacks. Despite Democratic victories in last week’s midterms, Trump is unlikely to change course. It would take budgetary and investigative pressure from Congress to make that change.

Julian E. Zelizer is a columnist at Foreign Policy and a professor of history and public affairs at Princeton University. He is the author of The Long View, a newsletter putting the news in perspective. In 2027, Norton will publish his new book, Rumble on the Promenade: The Clash of Justice and Power at the 1964 Convention. X: @julianzelizer

#6011. Rep. Ken Calvert wins all-Republican race in California

Rep. Ken Calvert defeated Rep. Young Kim in a redrawn Southern California district that pitted the two Republicans against one another.

Calvert was leading his rival by 7 points Monday night when The Associated Press called the race for California’s 40th District with more than 70 percent of the vote in.

Calvert, who chairs the powerful House Defense Appropriations Subcommittee, is the longest-serving Republican in the California delegation, first winning election to Congress in 1992.

The race was reshaped by the Golden State’s new voter-approved House map, drawn by state Democrats in response to mid-decade redistricting by Texas Republicans. The new map dismantled Calvert’s 41st District in Riverside County, transforming it into a safely blue Democratic seat in the Los Angeles area. That prompted him to run for the redrawn 40th District, which included a sizable percentage of his current constituents.

The rare intraparty general election was possible because Calvert and Kim finished in the top two slots in the state’s June primary. Under the California system, all candidates run on the same primary ballot, with the top two vote-getters, regardless of party, advancing to November.

Calvert had already declared victory last week, saying on social media that there was “no greater honor than serving my neighbors and our communities in Congress.”

Kim’s defeat is the second of her congressional career — she lost her initial bid during the 2018 blue wave before winning election to the House two years later.

In her concession message, Kim singled out California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom, who led the redistricting effort last year that targeted five Republican-held districts. Democrats flipped all five seats last week.

“It’s unfortunate that Gavin Newsom’s political redistricting scheme forced two Republican members from Congress into this race,’’ she said in a statement.

The race between was marked by rancor, with Calvert alleging that Kim was not a true conservative and supported higher taxes. Kim accused Calvert of growing rich off stock trades over his decades in Washington.

Calvert will serve in a delegation with a dramatically smaller GOP presence next year, with Democrats likely to hold 48 of California’s 52 House seats. Just two other California Republicans – Reps. Vince Fong and Tom McClintock – have been reelected so far, while a third, Rep. Jay Obernolte, narrowly leads his Democratic challenger in an as-yet-uncalled race.

The Calvert-Kim battle was not the only all-party November clash in California, with several districts featuring matchups between two Democrats.

One incumbent has already been unseated, with Rep. Jimmy Gomez losing to fellow Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres in the Los Angeles-area 34th District, according to The Associated Press.

Two other blue-on-blue contests in Northern California remained uncalled as of Tuesday afternoon: Rep. Mike Thompson was trailing venture capitalist Eric Jones in the 4th District, while Rep. Doris Matsui led Sacramento City Councilmember Mai Vang in the 7th District.

#6010. The Experts Are Taking Their Revenge Again

Analysis: The Experts Are Taking Their Revenge Again

At a political rally in Arizona in October, U.S. President Donald Trump joked that he “probably went a little too far” with the U.S.-Israeli military strikes against Iran that he initiated in February. The electoral catastrophe that unfolded for Republicans in the midterms a few weeks later made this abundantly clear.

During a midnight interview with Fox News at the end of election night on Nov. 3, when asked about what had hurt the GOP most at the polls, Trump conceded that “I think a part of it was Iran.” Setting aside equivocation the following day, Vice President J.D. Vance posted on X, “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. … And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

At a political rally in Arizona in October, U.S. President Donald Trump joked that he “probably went a little too far” with the U.S.-Israeli military strikes against Iran that he initiated in February. The electoral catastrophe that unfolded for Republicans in the midterms a few weeks later made this abundantly clear.

During a midnight interview with Fox News at the end of election night on Nov. 3, when asked about what had hurt the GOP most at the polls, Trump conceded that “I think a part of it was Iran.” Setting aside equivocation the following day, Vice President J.D. Vance posted on X, “The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. … And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

Energy prices had soared, and voters noticed that they weren’t being put first, punishing the incumbent party for this betrayal. The president’s most consequential foreign-policy mistake has turned out to be launching a war against a major regional power in the Middle East with a surfeit of misplaced optimism and scant consideration of what might go wrong. The irony does not need much teasing out.

It is not as if the president was not warned. As the New York Times journalists Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan detail in their book Regime Change, U.S. intelligence was skeptical of key elements of the case for war that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu presented to Trump at the White House Situation Room on Feb. 11.

Seeing upsides everywhere he looked, the Israeli prime minister said that Iran’s ballistic missile program would be destroyed in a few weeks, that a weakened Iran would be unable to close the Strait of Hormuz, and that the risk to neighboring states was small. He also reported that Mossad intelligence suggested that an intense bombing campaign would destabilize the regime, allowing Iranian opposition forces to assume control.

The CIA’s director, John Ratcliffe, reported back to the president and his principal advisors the next day. Agency analysts believed that military action could take out Iran’s leadership and destroy its ability to threaten its neighbors. But Ratcliffe said that the suggestion that airstrikes would spark regime change was “farcical,” according to the Times reporters. Secretary of State Marco Rubio stepped in to paraphrase: “In other words, it’s bullshit.” Vance strongly agreed. The chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Dan Caine, told Trump, “Sir, this is, in my experience, standard operating procedure for the Israelis. They oversell, and their plans are not always well-developed. They know they need us, and that’s why they’re hard-selling.” Warning lights were flashing everywhere.

Trump ultimately decided to authorize Operation Epic Fury on the basis that decapitating Iran’s leadership and striking decisively against its offensive capabilities was sufficient cause. It was a remarkable leap of faith for a man whose opposition to reckless foreign wars—Iraq, first and foremost—had helped him secure the Republican presidential nomination in 2016.

He restated this view in defeating President Joe Biden eight years later, too. At a campaign rally in Pennsylvania in October 2024, Trump said, “I will not send you to fight and die in a foolish, never-ending foreign war.” In launching war against Iran, Trump ignored private doubts expressed by his vice president, CIA director, secretary of state, and chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was the only person to unequivocally back war with Iran (which places him in a precarious position now.)

The history of U.S. foreign policy is replete with examples of influential and well-placed advisors ignoring or marginalizing compelling intelligence that contradicted their plans for war or escalation. In the case of the wars in Iraq and Vietnam, they also happen to correspond with the worst foreign-policy mistakes in American history. And just like Trump’s war against Iran, these were conflicts of choice, not of necessity, to deploy Richard Haass’s helpful binary. The rationales undergirding each war were different, but a common theme is present across all—ill-advised certainty defeated counterevidence and caution.

Determined to locate evidence that connected Saddam Hussein with al Qaeda’s 9/11 attacks, former Deputy Secretary of Defense Paul Wolfowitz repeatedly instructed the CIA to investigate the link and repeatedly got the same reply: No such relationship existed between this secular leader and the radical Islamist terrorist group.

The undersecretary of defense for policy, Douglas Feith, set up an alternative intelligence-gathering outfit, the Policy Counter Terrorism Evaluation Group, in the Pentagon to locate what the CIA had supposedly missed. It found nothing, but this did not stop Vice President Dick Cheney from insisting repeatedly that Saddam’s Iraq was linked to the 9/11 attacks, bolstering public support for any invasion of Iraq.

In late 2001 and through 2002, George Tenet’s CIA was browbeaten and ultimately marginalized as it failed to locate the smoking-gun evidence—both on weapons of mass destruction and Iraqi links with al Qaeda—that Bush administration hawks insisted would be there if only the agency looked hard enough. The war was launched in March 2003. Though the initial military action was ruthlessly effective—as was the case with U.S.-Israeli action against Iran in February—what happened after Saddam’s fall was not.

The August 1964 Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, which gave U.S. President Lyndon B. Johnson congressional authorization to wage war against North Vietnam, was predicated on a North Vietnamese attack on two U.S. destroyers that never actually happened. As LBJ later told Undersecretary of State George Ball, “Hell, those damn, stupid sailors were just shooting at flying fish.”

The resolution gave the Johnson administration ample latitude to do as it saw fit in Vietnam—LBJ said it was like “grandmother’s nightshirt. It covers everything.” Just two senators—Democrat Ernest Gruening from Alaska and Republican Wayne Morse from Oregon—voted against, warning their colleagues that they were effectively signing an undated declaration of war. Both men lost their next elections, but history has treated them kindly.

As the war escalated, Walt Rostow, one of the conflict’s key architects, was constantly at odds with intelligence analysts on how it was progressing. As Johnson’s national security advisor from April 1966, Rostow was in a powerful position to present his own spin on the intelligence reports that he received. He would cherry-pick small sections of good news in larger intelligence reports counseling caution and present his own optimistic summary to Johnson. As historian Arthur Schlesinger Jr. later remarked, “Intelligent people in the State Department have told me that Walt would funnel in the stuff that sustained his own thesis.” Rostow’s relationship with Langley understandably soured. When forwarding some raw eyewitness testimony to LBJ in the fall of 1967, Rostow wrote, “This is what the bombing of Hanoi and Haiphong really looks like—with all due respect to intelligence analysts 10,000 miles away.”

Rostow was certain that the U.S. bombing campaign against North Vietnam that he helped devise was winning the war and discounted intelligence that challenged his take. It was almost an article of faith for him.

The architects of the war against Iran in February held similar overconfidence in bombing’s coerciveness in an incredibly complex theater of operation. Airpower is indeed a crucial military tool, but unrealistic political goals—forcing North Vietnam to give up on its war of unification or forcing regime change in Tehran—are rarely achieved from the skies. Ignoring the intelligence that points this out simply invites failure.

Wolfowitz and Rostow were ideologues who believed they had finessed fundamental truths about the wars they strategized that the intelligence community had missed or refused to see. Trump’s worldview is very different to these two defense intellectuals—a Cold War liberal and a neoconservative—with their Ph.D.s from Chicago and Yale and scholarly books and publications.

But the certainty that Wolfowitz and Rostow held in the efficacy of the wars that they pushed in Iraq and Vietnam is mirrored by the confidence with which Trump launched his Iran misadventure. Few things are as dangerous in foreign policy as a powerful individual with undue confidence in a bad idea. And like Rostow and Wolfowitz, who did not later question the soundness of the advice that they dispensed, the president is not naturally predisposed to critical self-reflection.

“I would have done it again,” the president told reporters recently. It will be interesting to see how this position holds up as Iran becomes a critical flash point in the 2028 Republican primaries.

#6008. Senate Republicans plan 54-day blitz to push Trump's agenda before Democrats seize power

Senate Majority Leader John Thune discusses lessons he’s taking from the midterms and his future as the GOP’s leader in the U.S. Senate on ‘Special Report.’

With their leadership elections settled, Senate Republicans are gearing up to "maximize" their remaining time in power before Senate Democrats take over next year.

All eyes are again on Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., who was re-elected to another term as the Republican leader. Shortly after winning, Thune declared that he and the Senate GOP were "committed to being here to do whatever it takes to get as much done as we can."

"That means extending the calendar here, the number of days we're here, the number of hours we're here, the number of votes we may end up taking," Thune said. "But we are going to finish this legislative session strong."

SENATE GOP REBELLION FIZZLES AS THUNE KEEPS POWER DESPITE HISTORIC MIDTERM MASSACRE

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., conducts a news conference in the U.S. Capitol after winning the minority leader position for the 120th Congress in Senate Republican leadership elections on Nov. 10, 2026. (CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

The Senate was initially set to be in roughly 20 days from Tuesday until the changing of the guard, but Republicans are now squeezing the juice out of every last minute to ram through must-pass legislation, dozens of President Donald Trump’s nominees and more.

And Republicans agreed to hold themselves to that sprint until the end of the year at the tail end of their marathon closed-door meeting on Tuesday.

Lawmakers plan to "maximize the 54 days we have with congressional majorities, to confirm every judicial nominee and every executive nominee that the conference approves of, to pass our core Republican priorities, and to do everything humanly possible to pass a reconciliation bill before Jan. 3," according to a resolution agreed to in the meeting obtained by Fox News Digital.

Another crack at budget reconciliation could be the trickiest part of their ambitious year-end gauntlet, particularly depending on what lawmakers try to cram into the process.

GOP SENATOR WITHHOLDS SUPPORT FOR THUNE AS LEADERSHIP SHOWDOWN LOOMS

"I think we've got to keep it realistic to probably have any chance of passing, pretty narrow," Thune told Fox News Digital.

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., who chairs the Senate Budget Committee responsible for developing the scaffolding around the process, told Fox News Digital that he intended to present his plan to Republicans during their lunchtime meeting on Wednesday.

It’s also where Republicans are considering one last attempt at getting the SAVE America Act, or a version of it that could pass muster with the Senate rules referee.

"Oh yeah, that'd be part of it, you know, to provide funding for states for election integrity type of measures," Johnson said.

Defense funding will be another major task for Republicans, given that Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and Democrats are determined to use Congress’ power over the nation’s purse strings as a way to choke off spending on the Iran war.

SENATE REPUBLICAN PUSHES OVERHAUL TO CUT RED TAPE AND SPEED UP AMERICAN ENERGY PROJECTS

Senate Minority Leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., conducts a news conference at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee about Democrats taking control of the House and Senate in the midterm election on Nov. 4, 2026. (CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

Thune acknowledged that reconciliation could be another landing spot for Pentagon dollars to flow, but hoped Democrats would choose a different route.

"It's going to depend on whether or not they have any of their members who are persuaded that making sure that we have enough munitions and ammo and weaponry to be able to defend the country is a priority," Thune said. "I hope they do, in which case maybe we won't have to go down that path, but we're scoping it out right now."

One of the White House’s top priorities, and at the top of Thune’s to-do list, is confirming a slate of judicial and executive branch nominees. As of Tuesday, there were 23 judicial nominees, many of whom still needed to go through committee, and nearly 100 executive branch nominees that need confirmation.

There is a slew of other high-priority items that were punted to the lame duck, like the National Defense Authorization Act, a bipartisan permitting reform package and keeping the government funded.

Preventing another shutdown, or at least hammering out a deal, could be tricky given how the political winds shifted after the election.

Sen. Katie Britt, R-Ala., who serves on the Senate Appropriations Committee, told Fox News Digital that "where we can clear the decks, the better," to fund the government.

"I know that prior to the election that was the thought of some of our Democratic colleagues as well, but we have to be able to work together to get some of that done," Britt said.

Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

Could Israeli politics get more complicated? Israeli President Issac Herzog tapped Gadi Eisenkot over the weekend to form the next government. You would think that means the opposition parties led by Eisenkot—known in Israel as the “change bloc”—are on the verge of ousting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and forming a stable, centrist government. But that’s not quite the case, not yet anyway. As the haggling gets underway, let’s take a minute to lay out the facts—and sidestep the vitriol and virtue signaling that tends to dominate social media when it comes to Israel.

Based on the final results of the election held two weeks ago, Netanyahu and his bloc have 53 seats in the 120-seat parliament, while Eisenkot’s change bloc controls 48 seats. The remaining 19 seats belong to two Arab-led parties, the Joint List and Ra’am.

Could Israeli politics get more complicated? Israeli President Issac Herzog tapped Gadi Eisenkot over the weekend to form the next government. You would think that means the opposition parties led by Eisenkot—known in Israel as the “change bloc”—are on the verge of ousting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and forming a stable, centrist government. But that’s not quite the case, not yet anyway. As the haggling gets underway, let’s take a minute to lay out the facts—and sidestep the vitriol and virtue signaling that tends to dominate social media when it comes to Israel.

Based on the final results of the election held two weeks ago, Netanyahu and his bloc have 53 seats in the 120-seat parliament, while Eisenkot’s change bloc controls 48 seats. The remaining 19 seats belong to two Arab-led parties, the Joint List and Ra’am.

The nod from the president means that Eisenkot gets the first crack at forming a government. The clearest path to a majority would be for him to form a coalition with the Joint List and Ra’am. That would give the anti-Netanyahu forces a commanding 67-seat majority in Israel’s parliament—enough to address some of the most divisive issues in Israeli society, including expanding mandatory military service to include ultra-Orthodox Jews and establishing a state commission of inquiry into the security failures that led to Hamas’s attack on Oct. 7, 2023.

But things are never so straightforward, especially in Israeli politics. Theoretically, a change bloc government with the Joint List and Ra’am is possible, but there are informal barriers to getting there—and political traps once it is established—that would likely make the government unstable.

Since Israel’s founding, only one governing coalition included an Arab-led party, and it didn’t last long. In 2021, parties from across the political spectrum—united mainly by their antipathy for Netanyahu—formed a left-right coalition headed by Naftali Bennett, a onetime Netanyahu protégé. The coalition included Ra’am, which had focused mainly on bread-and-butter issues for Israel’s Arab citizens, who make up 20 percent of the population. In previous elections, the Arab-led parties were considered too fringe politically to be included in coalitions or they themselves ruled out serving in Israeli governments. Bennett’s decision to include Ra’am was groundbreaking.

But the motley coalition held together for just a year. The crisis that precipitated the government’s fall revolved around lawmakers from Ra’am and the left-wing Meretz party who opposed extending a procedural measure that benefitted settlers in the West Bank. This dispute within the coalition prompted the resignation of one of Bennett’s own deputies who assailed anti-Zionists—presumably Arab members—of the coalition holding the government “hostage.” Throughout this period, Netanyahu was able to capitalize on the government’s ideological diversity, adding to its stresses and strains by highlighting the contradictions between its right-wing and anti-Zionist members.

It is not clear why this time would be any different. A change bloc plus Arab parties would have the similar ideological fault lines. Perhaps the exigency of keeping Netanyahu out of the prime minister’s office would be enough to hold everyone together, but it would take significant political skill. All the discussion about a government with the Arab parties may be moot anyway. Eisenkot has laid down four conditions to be in the government—recognizing Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, strict adherence to the values laid out in Israel’s declaration of independence, mandatory national service for all, and recognition of Hamas as a terrorist organization. The first, second, and fourth conditions will be tough for the Joint List to agree to. Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas may have more flexibility, but he recently refused to call Hamas a terrorist organization.

I’m not sure how you square this circle. You can promise Arab parties lots of resources, and their leaders seem motivated to cooperate to prevent Netanyahu from returning to office. That is a good sign for the change bloc, but it does nothing to resolve the hard differences between Zionist and anti-Zionist parties.

The common knee-jerk reaction to this problem among social media posters and some members of the foreign-policy community is to declare Israel racist. Are there racists in Israel? No doubt there are. Right-wing politicians Avigdor Liberman, Bezalel Smotrich, Itamar Ben-Gvir, and others have a history of making racist anti-Arab comments. Netanyahu has repeatedly trafficked in fearmongering around the issue of Arab voters “racing to the ballots” during the elections. But to focus on racism alone is to miss the core tension of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Most Israeli Jews support the idea of Israel as a Jewish state, albeit with an Arab minority. It would be uncomfortable for them to have people in government who oppose the country’s founding principles and refuse to condemn Hamas.

At the same time, it should surprise no one that the leaders of Israel’s Arab parties have a different outlook and entirely different concerns. Arab Israelis have their own historical narrative, do not share Israel’s founding myths, and are not part of its collective memory.

One alternative is for Eisenkot to form a minority government without the Arab-led parties and rely on their support from the outside on crucial legislative votes. But minority governments tend to be unstable in Israel and at least one party within the change bloc, Liberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu (Israel Is Our Home), has ruled out such a configuration.

Another alternative would be for Eisenkot to invite the ultra-Orthodox (Haredi) parties to join his coalition. That seems to be more acceptable to mainstream Israelis, but barely. The white-hot anger directed at the Haredi parties among almost everyone in Israel is palpable. That is because most Haredi men do not serve in the military, and Israelis resent supporting an entire community that takes far more than it contributes to society. This would be a difficult coalition for Eisenkot to put together, though the leaders of the Ashkenazi Haredi party, United Torah Judaism, have indicated a willingness to consider it.

The fourth option is for Eisenkot to try and form a broad-based coalition with Netanyahu—what Israelis call a “national unity” government—with the two men rotating as prime ministers. That seems to be where Herzog wants to go. A Netanyahu-Eisenkot linkup would get to a majority in parliament easily and resolve several issues all at once for Israelis. The coalition would not include far-right figures Ben-Gvir and Smotrich, and there would be no need to cater to Haredi parties. The debate over normalizing the Arab-led parties by including them in a governing coalition would be put off for another day. Yet in the Rubik’s cube that is Israeli politics, this option also raises challenges.

For example, who would serve first as prime minister? And how would you guarantee that neither of them will violate the rotation agreement? Netanyahu did just that with the hapless Benny Gantz in 2020, bringing down the government and forcing new elections before Gantz could take over.

Beyond the procedures, Eisenkot would have to make the case to his voters why a deal with Netanyahu is warranted when opponents of Netanyahu hold 67 seats in the 120-member parliament. It is a tough argument to make, especially for Eisenkot, who said during the campaign that he would not agree to a national unity government with the man that he (and many others) hold responsible for failures that led to the Oct. 7 massacre.

Still, a so-called national unity government would probably be the most stable of all the options, freezing out parties on the margins and capturing that center-right part of the electorate where the preponderance of Jewish Israelis now live politically. It would also head off what many Israelis think of as the worst option of all—a political deadlock that leads to another election in the coming months.

Herzog has his job cut out for him if he wants to avoid another election, something that is to Netanyahu’s advantage but not to Israel’s. Wrangling Israel’s political parties is difficult even in the best of circumstances, especially for a president who has limited formal powers. Herzog will rely on the dignity of his office and his powers of persuasion to get an outcome that, regardless of its content, is likely to make a significant number of Israelis unhappy. In the coming weeks, being Israel’s president is going to be among the worst jobs in the world.

Steven A. Cook is a columnist at Foreign Policy and the Eni Enrico Mattei senior fellow for Middle East and Africa studies at the Council on Foreign Relations. His latest book is The End of Ambition: America’s Past, Present, and Future in the Middle East. X: @stevenacook

#6005. FIRST ON FOX: Supreme Court justices confront what it will take to keep America's founding freedoms alive

Justices Brett Kavanaugh, Neil Gorsuch and Amy Coney Barrett reflect on America's founding principles and urge Americans to embrace civic education and engagement to preserve the nation's freedoms for future generations. (Federalist Society)

FIRST ON FOX: As America celebrates 250 years of independence this year, three conservative Supreme Court justices are warning that preserving the nation's founding freedoms for future generations depends on Americans understanding their history, embracing civic education and actively participating in their system of government.

Justices Brett Kavanaugh, Neil Gorsuch and Amy Coney Barrett each implored Americans to familiarize themselves with their system of government and the history behind it to ensure that the nation’s legacy is preserved.

Though the three conservative justices were united in their call for civic education, they each approached the topic differently in a series of interviews filmed by the Federalist Society and obtained by Fox News Digital. The videos come ahead of the Federalist Society's 2026 National Lawyers Convention this week, which spotlights "250 Years of American Exceptionalism."

Gorsuch, for instance, struck a distinctly religious tone.

GORSUCH HIGHLIGHTS STAGGERING DECLINE IN CIVIC LITERACY THAT PROMPTED HIM TO AUTHOR NEW BOOK

Supreme Court Justices Amy Coney Barrett, Brett Kavanaugh and Neil Gorsuch discussing America's 250th anniversary. (Federalist Society)

"I think it's very easy to take the rights granted in our Constitution and the ideals expressed in the Declaration for granted," he said. "They are, for us, a little bit like the air we breathe and the water a fish might swim in. They seem natural to us, but they weren't in 1776. The ideas in the Declaration of Independence that all of us are created equal, that every one of us has God-given rights — they don't come from government, they come from God."

Gorsuch, who was appointed to the court by President Donald Trump in 2017 following the death of Justice Antonin Scalia, went on to describe the importance of historical study to the preservation of the American way of life.

THE UNWINNABLE WAR AMERICA'S FOUNDING FATHERS FOUGHT AND WON CHANGED HUMAN HISTORY FOREVER

Chief Justice of the Supreme Court John Roberts, Justice Elena Kagan, Justice Brett Kavanaugh, Justice Amy Coney Barrett and retired Justice Anthony Kennedy attend President Donald Trump's address to a joint session of Congress at the U.S. Capitol on March 4, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Win McNamee/Pool via REUTERS)

"Our country is a blessing from God, and that we owe great thanks for it, and we have great responsibility for it," he went on. "The reason why our Constitution and Declaration have survived is because people choose it anew in every generation. You need to know its history. You need to know what you're preserving. Daniel Webster said it took 6,000 years for us to generate a system of government like this. Don't expect that to happen easily or again."

Kavanaugh, similarly, emphasized the importance of education.

"I think our education system is absolutely fundamental to ensuring that in the next 250 years, we preserve this republic and improve upon this republic. So, teaching American history, teaching the values of this country, the history of this country, why this country exists, how this country has been preserved, how this country has been improved over time, for example, by our constitutional amendment process and otherwise," the justice, appointed to the bench following a tumultuous confirmation process in 2018, said.

"And I think all of us should be constantly striving to ensure civics education, not only for our youth, but for all of us, and that we constantly are learning and participating in our system of government," he continued.

SPEAKER JOHNSON WARNS STUDENTS ARE 'INDOCTRINATED' TO SEE US THROUGH 'WRONG LENSES' AS NATION CELEBRATES 250TH

John Roberts, chief justice of the U.S. Supreme Court, from left, Elena Kagan, associate justice of the U.S. Supreme Court, Brett Kavanaugh, associate justice of the U.S. Supreme Court, and Amy Coney Barrett, associate justice of the U.S. Supreme Court, during a State of the Union address in the House chamber of the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday, Feb. 24, 2026. (Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The Federalist Society filmed its interviews ahead of its National Lawyers Convention, which will bring together minds from across the conservative legal movement to discuss matters deemed pressing.

While not interviewed by the Federalist Society, Justice Sonia Sotomayor shared her thoughts on America's 250th anniversary during an event at Mount Vernon's Washington Library, taking a slightly darker tone than her conservative colleagues.

During her talk, which centered primarily on civic engagement, Sotomayor argued that the United States is in a rough place at the moment and that it would take "some hard work" for it to get back on an "even keel."

"There are some norms we may have lost forever," she said. "But I don’t think that we will fail as a democracy. But I think we’re going to have a hard patch figuring out what that means."

Barrett, meanwhile, focused on the Declaration of Independence and how she believes it should inspire civic participation today.

"We're not passive observers in the American project. We're participants in it. It is our project," she said. "I might suggest that people look at the last line of the Declaration of Independence. It ends with a mutual pledge in which the signatories to the document mutually pledge their lives, their fortunes and their sacred honor to the success of the American project. And they made good on that promise. Some lost their fortune, lost their property to loyalists ... and they pledged with their honor not to deviate from the commitments that they had made in signing the Declaration of Independence."

"Surely that's the kind of commitment that it takes to have it keep going forward," said Barrett.

#6004. Jim Jordan picked as new minority leader for House GOP

House Republicans on Tuesday opted for a new face atop their ranks, electing Rep. Jim Jordan as the incoming minority leader for the 120th Congress after Republicans suffered massive losses in last week’s midterm elections.

The Ohio Republican defeated outgoing Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., in a closed-door, secret-ballot election. The final tally was 106-73.

“Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families. Democrats offer more government. We will offer more freedom,” Jordan said after the hourslong process.

The two had been working the phones before making their pitches during a candidates forum in the Capitol Visitor Center’s auditorium on Tuesday morning. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., announced last week he would not seek a leadership post in the new Congress, which will be seated on Jan. 3.

“Obviously Jim and I know each other, but I’ve got a proven record of how to bring people together,” Scalise said ahead of the vote, trying to play up his experience, including more than a decade on the leadership team that included a stint as whip.

As House Republicans trickled out of the candidates’ forum for breaks or to take phone calls, one member, granted anonymity to discuss a private session, said Scalise and Jordan “both have strong points, but they both have flaws.” Each made an unsuccessful bid for speaker in 2023 after the ouster of Kevin McCarthy, before the gavel ultimately went to Johnson.

Declining to reveal which would get his vote, the member said: “I won’t talk about a secret vote, but I know who I think is best to lead us.”

The incoming minority conference also selected other leaders on Tuesday.

Majority Whip Tom Emmer of Minnesota held off a challenge from Texas Rep. August Pfluger to become minority whip in January, despite some grumbling about how tight votes were handled on the floor this year.

“We’ve got to retool our whip operation,” Texas Rep. Nathaniel Moran said Tuesday morning, pointing to “the number of times we were held up by either discharge petitions or failed rule votes.”

“Those were things that should not have happened in the majority,” said Moran as he publicly backed Pfluger for whip.

But Emmer projected confidence after his whip win, comparing the moment to when Republicans were down and out after their losses in 2018 only to rebound a few years later.

“To our colleagues on the left, enjoy this honeymoon phase, because come Jan. 3, 2027, you will regret ever putting your name on a ballot,” he said at a news conference, adding that Republicans under his watch would expose the “empty promises” that Democrats made to voters and push back on what he called their “radical” agenda.

In the day’s only three-way race, conference Chair Lisa McClain of Michigan defeated Reps. Erin Houchin of Indiana and Greg Steube of Florida to keep her spot.

“We had a spirited leadership election. There were important conversations about the future of our conference, and I listened,” McClain said at the news conference.

In the race to lead House Republicans’ campaign arm, Rep. Brian Jack of Georgia defeated Rep. Rudy Yakym of Indiana, seen as an up-and-coming Ways and Means Committee member. That means Jack will take on a huge share of the uphill task of selecting candidates and raising funds for the 2028 cycle as he helms the National Republican Congressional Committee.

But most of the attention heading into Tuesday’s closed-door proceedings was on the minority leader race.

Johnson, the outgoing speaker, declined to endorse a candidate but had encouraging words for Jordan after his win. “He’s going to do an excellent job. He’s a good, trusted friend and brother,” he said.

Rep. Tom Cole, R-Okla., said it was a “tough choice for the conference to make,” but he wasn’t disappointed in the pick. “He was an exceptionally capable chairman of both Oversight and Judiciary. He’s excellent in an interview,” Cole said of Jordan. “He’s got boundless energy and determination.”

Jordan’s victory means he will form a political and legal tag team with newly installed White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller in pushing back on a number of investigations House Democrats have planned for President Donald Trump, some of his second-term administration officials and his business-minded family members.

Democrats will have more than 250 seats in the chamber, with a number of races still uncalled. Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, expected to become the next House speaker, told reporters last week he predicts Democrats will have at least 255 seats when all the ballots have been counted and verification processes have played out.

“It’s a historic majority in the 21st century,” Jeffries told reporters in Washington, D.C., the day after the midterms. “The American people have chosen the economy over extremism. The American people have chosen hope over hatred. The American people have chosen common sense over corruption, chaos and cruelty. The American people have chosen House Democrats because they want to see a dramatic change in direction.”

Political analysts have predicted an internal battle within the GOP for the direction the party takes over the next two years — and after Trump leaves office in January 2029.

The Institute for Legislative Analysis, a nonprofit organization that advocates to shrink the size and influence of the government, released a vote study assessment on Monday. Its calculations led ILA to endorse Emmer and three fresh faces: Jordan, Steube and Jack.

“It’s clear many Republican voters feel their representatives in Washington aren’t representing them,” Ryan McGowan, the institute’s CEO, said in a statement. “It will be interesting to see whether House Republicans respond by choosing leaders … whose voting records are much more closely aligned with the party’s conservative base.”

Several GOP sources late last week, granted anonymity to be candid, said they were expecting a close outcome between Scalise and Jordan, adding Emmer was working the phones hard to remain whip. One said having either Scalise or Jordan atop the conference, with the expectation of Emmer staying on as whip, “won’t be much of a change at the top.”

The new leadership team will take over Jan. 3, when Democrats are expected to, in part, use their large majority to target all things Trump 2.0. The same GOP source said the majority party will “inevitably be pursuing impeachment by August recess despite their disciplined statements to the media pre-election.”

Trump replied in the affirmative when a “60 Minutes” correspondent asked him in an interview that aired Sunday night if he could work with Democrats, should they also be aggressively investigating his team.

“Well, I did it for four years,” the president said of his first term. “They impeached me twice. And there are those that say that worked out to my advantage.”

Nina Heller, Michael Macagnone and Samantha Freeman contributed to this report.

#6002. It’s Possible to Fix the United Nations

Argument: It’s Possible to Fix the United Nations

International order is not the absence of conflict, nor is it the rigid defense of the status quo. Rather, it is the existence of predictable mechanisms to manage inevitable disagreements. And the primary mechanism tasked with upholding international peace and security—the United Nations Security Council (UNSC)—is no longer fit for purpose.

The UNSC still resembles the world of 1945, giving privileged status to the victors of World War II and the holders of colonial empires. Without reform to give rising and middle powers a status commensurate with their growing influence, states will eventually see more sense in pursuing their security interests unilaterally or through exclusive, destabilizing blocs. For now, with a few notable exceptions, states remain committed to speaking the language of multilateralism. But make no mistake: Reforming the UNSC is not a matter of aesthetics or desirability; it is an absolute necessity.

International order is not the absence of conflict, nor is it the rigid defense of the status quo. Rather, it is the existence of predictable mechanisms to manage inevitable disagreements. And the primary mechanism tasked with upholding international peace and security—the United Nations Security Council (UNSC)—is no longer fit for purpose.

The UNSC still resembles the world of 1945, giving privileged status to the victors of World War II and the holders of colonial empires. Without reform to give rising and middle powers a status commensurate with their growing influence, states will eventually see more sense in pursuing their security interests unilaterally or through exclusive, destabilizing blocs. For now, with a few notable exceptions, states remain committed to speaking the language of multilateralism. But make no mistake: Reforming the UNSC is not a matter of aesthetics or desirability; it is an absolute necessity.

Three dynamics have held up reform. But each may be slowly giving way, creating a rare window for genuine change.

The first and most commonly cited obstacle is the Security Council’s five permanent veto-wielding members, or P5—the United States, China, Russia, France, and the United Kingdom. The P5 countries are wary of admitting rising powers as fellow veto wielders, as it would diminish their own influence in the body and make it more susceptible to deadlock.

However, without reform, the council’s legitimacy in the eyes of the global majority will deteriorate, rendering it more and more irrelevant. The P5 will be the biggest losers if the UNSC fades into insignificance, as they have the most to lose: their veto prerogatives. Consequently, the P5 are only likely to allow for reform when the council appears to be nearing the brink of collapse—a point that the world may soon approach if the P5 continue to wield their vetoes with impunity.

The second issue is the deadlock between the two main reform groupings: the G4 coalition of Germany, Japan, Brazil, and India, which favor enlarging the permanent membership of the UNSC to include themselves, and the Uniting for Consensus group, which favors only adding additional elected seats to the council. The uncompromising competition between these two blocs has prevented other proposals from gaining steam. However, Germany’s recent failed bid for a two-year term on the council has put into question the viability of its claim to a permanent seat—and the viability of the G4 proposal as a whole. This enables a possible shake-up that allows for the emergence of new and more creative reform ideas.

The third factor is that discussions over which reform model would best enhance the UNSC’s efficiency, effectiveness, and legitimacy has, to date, been largely speculative. Neither side has been able to predict with any meaningful accuracy the implications of their proposed reforms.

This, too, is now changing. Thanks to artificial intelligence, complex simulations can be conducted that calculate potential shifts in the council’s performance. We have conducted such a simulation to determine precisely what each proposal would achieve—and what it would risk. The simulation shows that the G4 model would dramatically increase gridlock over the next five decades. Council business would slow down as decision-making speed per resolution would grow from 28.5 days to 42.1 days, and veto use would grow by more than 60 percent. Despite giving them a seat at the table, the resulting paralysis would encourage leading powers to work outside the UNSC, defeating the purpose of reform entirely.

Yet while the Uniting for Consensus group’s proposal would limit the damage to the council’s efficiency and effectiveness, it fails to resolve its legitimacy deficit. The UNSC cannot effectively serve as a long-term custodian of the international order if Britain continues to enjoy a more privileged position than India—the world’s most populous country and likely soon to be its third-largest economy.

How, then, to resolve this conundrum? The AI simulation points to two mechanisms.

First, if more countries are to gain the veto, then this must be balanced by creating a veto override mechanism: for example, a veto wielder must secure one or two concurring negative votes among sitting council members, otherwise, a two-thirds majority in the General Assembly can overturn the veto.

The simulation shows that this would reduce veto usage by up to 40 percent, even before any cast vetoes are overturned. It would also speed up decision-making on average from 28.5 days to 21 days because veto wielders would either know that they have the necessary concurring vote(s) and cast their veto without delay, or know that they don’t and be incentivized to compromise to avoid a potentially humiliating General Assembly override.

Skeptics argue that the P5 countries are unlikely to agree to any reform that dilutes their veto privileges. But the simulation projects that successful overrides would occur only 28 percent of the time (or as low as 14 percent of the time, if the vote to override takes place by public roll call rather than by secret ballot). Agreeing to this limited mechanism, which would only take effect when a great power is isolated to the point of having no allies on an expanded council, is a small price to pay to ensure the council’s long-term legitimacy—and the permanent members’ privileged position that comes with it.

Second, a pool of “semipermanent” members, serving multiple lengthy terms and rotating on and off the council a few countries at a time, would offer middle powers that fail to earn a permanent seat a substantial consolation prize. According to the simulation, it would also triple small states’ likelihood of election to an ordinary council seat by taking these middle powers out of the running.

Countries such as Japan, Brazil, Argentina, India, and Pakistan currently monopolize the council’s nonpermanent seats, serving on average more than one term per decade, leaving smaller countries to earn a place only once every 30-50 years. The simulation shows that this proposal, if tabled by a strong coalition of small and developing states, has a 78 percent chance of being adopted and contributing to breaking the logjam.

The “international order” may be an abstract concept, but it takes concrete form in the institutions through which states manage their differences, constrain the use of force, and prevent conflict from descending into chaos. None matters more than the UNSC.

For decades, the presumed trade-off between legitimacy and effectiveness has been an obstacle to meaningful reform. Our simulations suggest that this is a false choice: A more representative council can also be a more effective one. What is, in fact, impossible is a new and stable order without a Security Council designed for it.

Zachary Paikin is the deputy director of the Better Order Project at the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft.

Trita Parsi is the executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft. X: @tparsi

#6001. Bessent moved to military base as Iran threats exceed ‘advanced stage,’ official says

Secretary of State Marco Rubio argued Tuesday that economic pressure on Iran eliminates the need for major combat operations.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been relocated from his home in Washington, D.C., to a military base amid Iranian assassination threats this week, a senior administration official confirmed to Fox News.

Tehran has ramped up its efforts to target senior U.S. officials overseas, with White House chief of staff Stephen Miller and Secretary of State Marco Rubio also relocating to military or protected housing in recent weeks.

The senior official told Fox that threats against Bessent had reached "more than an advanced stage." The official declined to say when exactly Bessent was relocated.

Bessent has played a central role in the economic battle against Iran, launching "Operation Economic Outcast" this summer in an effort to isolate Iran's economy from the rest of the world.

COULD IRAN’S REGIME COLLAPSE? EXPERTS ASSESS BESSENT’S BID TO SEVER FINANCIAL LIFELINES

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent speaks to reporters outside the White House in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday, Nov. 5, 2025. (Eric Lee/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Bessent said the wave of sanctions would bring about the "asphyxiation" of Iran's economy.

The Treasury Department confirmed Bessent's departure in a statement to Fox News on Tuesday, adding that the secretary refuses to "be deterred by the Iranian regime’s threats."

The New York Times first reported Bessent's relocation, citing three anonymous sources.

IRAN HAS 'SUBSTANTIALLY INCREASED' EFFORTS TO TARGET AMERICANS ABROAD, US INTELLIGENCE MEMO WARNS

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, President Donald Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth speak during a cabinet meeting at the White House in Washington, D.C., on Thursday, March 26, 2026. Trump threatened Iran with intensified military action after Tehran rejected Washington's push for a peace deal, with the two sides far apart in efforts to end the near monthlong war. "We don't need to conduct military strikes if we're achieving the same objective through economic means and economic pressure," Rubio told reporters.

He rejected the suggestion that the U.S. and Iran were at a stalemate, arguing that sanctions, the naval blockade and other measures were steadily weakening Tehran.

TRUMP BETS ECONOMIC PRESSURE CAN SQUEEZE IRAN AS REGIME’S OWN FAILURES DEEPEN THE PAIN

White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller speaks during a press briefing at the White House, Thursday, May 1, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (AP Photo/Alex Brandon)

"They’re bleeding. They’re bleeding economically," Rubio said. "It is an increased pressure on Iran that continues to grow every day."

The push comes a week after an election in which the war proved a political liability for Republicans.

#5999. Hegseth’s Leadership Has Damaged the Pentagon

On Monday, U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie introduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, triggering a vote in the House of Representatives that could come as early as this week. Massie, a Republican who will leave Congress in January, accuses Hegseth of waging an “unlawful” war in Iran and abusing the office. Hegseth will be the first civilian leader of the U.S. military establishment to face impeachment in 150 years.

The last, William Belknap, was President Ulysses S. Grant’s secretary of war—the title at the time for the civilian leader of the U.S. Army, before a unified Defense Department. The House voted unanimously to impeach him. Belknap resigned ahead of his Senate trial; he avoided conviction because of many senators’ discomfort with impeaching a private citizen. (Impeachments do not require the accused to be in office.)
