Massie, a Republican who will leave Congress in January, accuses Hegseth of waging an “unlawful” war in Iran and abusing the office. Hegseth will be the first civilian leader of the U.S. military establishment to face impeachment in 150 years.

The last, William Belknap, was President Ulysses S. Grant’s secretary of war—the title at the time for the civilian leader of the U.S. Army, before a unified Defense Department. The House voted unanimously to impeach him. Belknap resigned ahead of his Senate trial; he avoided conviction because of many senators’ discomfort with impeaching a private citizen. (Impeachments do not require the accused to be in office.)

Massie’s charge sheet includes eight counts, the most severe of which is that Hegseth “knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders to initiate war against a foreign nation notwithstanding the absence of congressional authorization” and “demonstrated that he will remain a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office.”

Four of the counts of impeachment involve war powers, while the others concern civilian casualties, extrajudicial killings during boat strikes, suppressing free speech, and kidnapping a foreign leader.

The indictment does not include some of Hegseth’s more egregious norm- and law-violating behavior: violating the Impoundment Control Act by refusing to release funds authorized and appropriated by Congress for aid to Ukraine, requiring uniformed military participation in partisan rallies, refusing briefings to congressional Democrats, denying press access to the Pentagon, firing without explanation more than two dozen senior officers confirmed by the Senate in their ranks and positions, appointing people forced out of military service for insubordination or political acts to senior civilian positions in the Defense Department, renaming the department without congressional authorization, and campaigning against sitting members of Congress.

President Donald Trump continues to support Hegseth, praising him for “winning two wars.” And the defense secretary continues undaunted: On Nov. 5, he released a nearly six-minute video insisting that “this is not about me, but of course, the other side, in case you’ve noticed, they’re obsessed. A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly, just like they tried against President Trump twice.”

The defense secretary’s most important responsibility is managing Congress because under the U.S. Constitution, it is Congress that has the power to “raise and support Armies” and “provide and maintain a Navy.” Hegseth has poisoned those relationships. It is likely that his impeachment will be successful in the House on at least the count of attempting to penalize the speech of Sen. Mark Kelly, whom Hegseth groundlessly accused of sedition. (Hegseth has initiated proceedings to retroactively reduce Kelly’s military rank and retirement pay.)

Rep. James Comer, the Republican chairman of the House oversight committee, sounds dubious about defending Hegseth rather than supportive, saying that “there are a lot of questions” about the defense secretary. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is a “hard yes” on impeachment. Tennessee Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn appears unlikely to give Hegseth an exit with honor by appointing him to her vacant Senate seat.

Trump will surely goad Hegseth on to fight the impeachment and behave outrageously—both as a distraction from the drubbing of the Republicans in the midterm elections and to indulge his entertainment approach to governance since it would be “great television.”

Whether or not Hegseth is convicted, his actions have already cost the Defense Department years of combat-tested experience in the senior leaders who were forced out and have instilled a chilling effect on those who remain.

Hegseth has eroded military readiness by poor planning for the Iran war, requiring extended deployments; robbed the force of funding by failing to gain congressional support for a war supplemental spending bill; continued munitions shortfalls because he structured the budget to pay for them in expectation of a third partisan reconciliation bill; damaged retention in the force, as 53 percent of service members now want to leave earlier because of politicization; and caused allies to question the legality of U.S. military operations.

There will be a strong temptation among Hegseth’s adversaries to bring the military into the impeachment process by calling fired officers to testify as witnesses.

This would be a mistake, both normatively and practically. As a normative matter, it damages civil-military relations to place the military in the position of judging its civilian masters. What a democracy should want in febrile political moments is for the military to remain politically inert. Practically, what some envision as a long table of uniformed officers with glittering medals bearing witness to policy depredations would actually be a parade of suits explaining that they have no idea why they were relieved or forced into retirement.

The two fundamental tests of whether the U.S. model of civil-military relations is healthy are that the political leadership can fire any military officer and that the military will carry out the civilian leadership’s policies whether or not it agrees with the decisions. For all the destruction that Hegseth has visited upon the U.S. military, its professional adherence to subordination to civilian control remains strong.

That is yet one more reason the military deserves much better civilian leadership than Trump, the senators who confirmed Hegseth as defense secretary, and Hegseth himself have provided.

Kori Schake is a senior fellow and the director of foreign and defense policy studies at the American Enterprise Institute. She is the author of The State and the Soldier: A History of Civil-Military Relations in the United States. X: @KoriSchake

#5998. Rep. Darren Soto survives Republican-drawn map in Florida

Florida Rep. Darren Soto, the most vulnerable House Democrat running for reelection, narrowly won a sixth term Tuesday in a district that state Republicans redrew in their favor.

Soto was leading Republican Navy veteran Dan Green by less than a point when The Associated Press called the race for Central Florida’s 9th District a week after Election Day. His margin of victory was above the 0.5 percent threshold that would trigger a recount under state law.

House Democrats have so far flipped more than 40 seats and appear on track to hold their biggest majority in the chamber in decades. Soto’s win means that no House Democratic incumbent lost to a Republican in the general election this year. And Florida Democrats defended all four seats the GOP had hoped to pick up under the state’s new Republican-drawn map.

Democratic Reps. Kathy Castor and Jared Moskowitz both won reelection from districts that shifted red, while Democrat Pia Dandiya, a former high school principal, defeated Republican Marine Corps veteran Casey Askar for a redrawn open seat in South Florida.

Soto, who declared victory last week, had been seen as the most vulnerable of the targeted Florida Democrats. The new map reduced the Hispanic population of his district as the seat shifted from one that Kamala Harris would have carried in 2024 to one that Donald Trump would have taken by 18 points.

“Despite the Florida Republican legislature’s efforts to redraw me out of this district, my record of delivering for Florida showed voters that I am a reliable fighter for them in Congress,” Soto said in a Nov. 4 statement.

In a Tuesday memo detailing how House Democrats secured their historic majority, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee took aim at Republicans’ mid-decade redistricting efforts, saying their “attempts to steal seats … supremely backfired.”

While Florida Republicans were unsuccessful in flipping the four Democrat-held seats, the party held all of its House seats in the Sunshine State. Republican Rep. María Elvira Salazar narrowly won reelection in the Miami-area 27th District over Democratic challenger Eliott Rodriguez, the AP reported Tuesday. In the 7th District outside Orlando, Republican former TV news anchor Ryan Elijah defeated Democratic Navy veteran Bale Dalton, a former NASA chief of staff who conceded Tuesday.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the chances of a U.S.-Iran peace deal, a suspected Chinese spy targeting Nvidia, and the elephant in the room at COP31.

U.S. President Donald Trump hosted Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani at the White House on Monday as part of ongoing efforts to avoid a fresh round of U.S. strikes on Iran. But as Washington and Tehran remain unwilling to make concessions to end the war, senior officials appear to be pessimistic about the likelihood of an imminent peace deal.

Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the chances of a U.S.-Iran peace deal, a suspected Chinese spy targeting Nvidia, and the elephant in the room at COP31.

U.S. President Donald Trump hosted Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani at the White House on Monday as part of ongoing efforts to avoid a fresh round of U.S. strikes on Iran. But as Washington and Tehran remain unwilling to make concessions to end the war, senior officials appear to be pessimistic about the likelihood of an imminent peace deal.

“I wouldn’t say we’re at the verge of a breakthrough,” U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said ahead of Monday’s talks.

Last week, Iranian officials announced, via Qatari mediators, a two-day plan to build mutual trust. Day one would have the U.S. military lift its naval blockade on Iranian ports and release some of Tehran’s frozen assets. In exchange, Iran would invite the International Atomic Energy Agency to send inspectors to its bombed nuclear sites. Day two would then see the Strait of Hormuz reopened, after which nuclear talks would resume.

There is a caveat, though: Washington must first agree to Tehran’s seven conditions for ending the war, including canceling new U.S. sanctions on Iran and reinstating U.S. oil waivers.

Speaking on Sunday, Rubio characterized Iran’s conditions as “not just unacceptable, but in some cases, outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic.”

The U.S. president told CNN on Sunday that it is “highly unlikely” that he will order the U.S. military to return to all-out war. “It depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement,” Trump said.

Iranian state media accused the United States of firing “projectiles” at the strategic Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday. Tehran also issued a warning to the United States that same day. “Our 2-day proposal stands: meet the requirements, including end to war on all fronts, and you will see results,” Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi wrote on X, adding, “Or choose war, and see our alert and battle-hardened Warriors rain down hell.”

Such threats have made other Persian Gulf powers doubt the effectiveness of current peace talks. The region should “prepare for a long period of uncertainty in which neither a decisive resolution nor stable regional order can be taken for granted,” senior Emirati official Anwar Gargash told Reuters on Monday.

Tuesday, Nov. 10: The United Arab Emirates hosts two-day trilateral talks involving Russia, Ukraine, and the United States.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen visits Bulgaria.

Wednesday, Nov. 11: Spain’s largest unions hold a general strike.

Russia hosts a leaders’ meeting of the Collective Security Treaty Organization.

Thursday, Nov. 12: Danish lawmakers consider the joint defense agreement between Greenland and the United States.

Sunday, Nov. 15: The Philippines kicks off a three-day Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit.

Cape Verde holds a presidential election.

Alleged China ties. Nvidia stocks plummeted as much as 8.8 percent during trading on Monday after CEO Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair with a woman who is suspected of being a Chinese spy. The company’s board stressed over the weekend that there is “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.” Still, the U.S.-based corporation plans to open an immediate investigation into the incident. Jensen will continue to lead the company during the inquiry.

This past spring, Rubio drafted a classified memo warning top Trump administration officials that the Nvidia CEO was in a romantic relationship with a woman named Alice Huang whom U.S. intelligence sources believe had been recruited to spy by China’s State Security Ministry. Alice Huang was the CEO of a Singapore-based data center company, Megaspeed, that the U.S. Commerce Department had investigated on suspicion that it was helping China smuggle in Nvidia’s restricted artificial intelligence chips. It is unclear if she is still employed at Megaspeed.

Jensen Huang is one of the world’s most consequential figures in the AI industry and an influential ally of Trump. Following news of Huang’s affair, Trump called Huang an “honorable guy” who has done “an amazing job for our country,” and he confirmed that he still plans to take Huang on his upcoming trip to China. On Monday, Beijing denied the espionage allegations.

Missing from COP31. This year’s United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) kicked off in the Turkish city of Antalya on Monday against a global backdrop of deadly flooding, surging fuel costs, and record-setting temperatures. The 12-day event is expected to prioritize curbing greenhouse gas emissions and advancing climate legislation.

“We want people to feel the results of climate ‌talks in ⁠daily life: in buildings that use less energy, in clean public transport, in energy they can afford, and in new jobs,” Turkish COP31 President Murat Kurum said on Monday.

However, with the leaders of world’s top three carbon dioxide emitters—China, the United States, and India—not attending the event, experts expect that this year’s summit could amount to little. Other notable absences include Russian President Vladimir Putin, French President Emmanuel Macron, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni. In fact, only a few of the 91 world leaders attending COP31 come from industrialized nations with significant carbon footprints.

Heading home? Ousted Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina requested new identity documents, including a passport, on Monday to enable her return from self-imposed exile in India, according to a letter seen by Reuters.

“If death is my destiny, I would rather die on the soil of my own country, among my own people,” Hasina told The Associated Press last week. Dhaka, however, has rejected her request, saying that it will not give a “passport to a terrorist.” Bangladesh’s war crimes court sentenced Hasina to death in absentia in November 2025 for her deadly crackdown on student-led protests in the summer of 2024, during which as many as 1,400 people were killed, according to U.N. estimates.

Hasina “is a fugitive criminal,” said Humaiun Kobir, Bangladesh’s state minister for foreign affairs. “We have an active extradition treaty with India. We want her handed over,” he added. New Delhi has yet to comment on Hasina’s request and Dhaka’s refusal. Previously, though, India has refused to surrender Hasina to Bangladeshi authorities, straining diplomatic ties between the neighboring nations.

On Sunday, a modern synagogue in Budapest transformed—for one night only—into a runway for Orthodox Jewish women hoping to challenge stereotypes about their modest dress code. Under that dress code, known as tzniut, Orthodox Jewish women are generally required to cover their collarbones, elbows, and knees; the rules also dictate that married women must cover their hair. Although some outsiders view these policies as restrictive, the organizers of the “Kosher & Chic” fashion show aimed to show that women can still dress to reflect their personalities while following modesty rules.

#5994. What to Know About Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s Chinese Spy Scandal

Explainer: What to Know About Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s Chinese Spy Scandal

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

Nvidia, the United States’ foremost national champion in its effort to lead the global technology race, has been rocked by a scandal surrounding CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.

Huang admitted to the affair in an email to Nvidia’s 42,000-plus employees on Sunday, apologizing to his wife and children for the “hurt” his infidelity caused as well as to the company and its employees. “Leading Nvidia is the privilege of my life,” Huang wrote. “My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to Nvidia and will work to earn back your confidence.”

Nvidia, the United States’ foremost national champion in its effort to lead the global technology race, has been rocked by a scandal surrounding CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.

Huang admitted to the affair in an email to Nvidia’s 42,000-plus employees on Sunday, apologizing to his wife and children for the “hurt” his infidelity caused as well as to the company and its employees. “Leading Nvidia is the privilege of my life,” Huang wrote. “My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to Nvidia and will work to earn back your confidence.”

The affair has implications far beyond Huang and his family. As the world’s leading producer of advanced semiconductor chips used to power artificial intelligence models and data centers, Nvidia has become a critical node in U.S. national security; meanwhile, the global demand for its products has seen the company’s valuation balloon to more than $4 trillion. Export restrictions on Nvidia’s most advanced chips—particularly to China—have become a cornerstone of U.S. technology policy, and Huang has developed a close relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump over the past two years.

The allegations first became public on Oct. 29, when the New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence had concluded that a Chinese businesswoman believed to be spying on behalf of Beijing had developed a “close relationship” with the Nvidia chief executive.

The woman, Alice Huang (also known as Huang Le), was an executive at the Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed. According to U.S. intelligence, she was recruited by China’s main intelligence agency, the Ministry of State Security, to gather information on Jensen Huang and help China gain access to Nvidia’s most advanced chips, which have been restricted by U.S. export controls since 2022.

Megaspeed had previously been investigated by the U.S. Commerce Department on suspicion that it was helping to smuggle Nvidia’s AI chips into China, a claim that Megaspeed has denied. A statement from December 2025 posted on the company’s website says investigations by the U.S. government and Nvidia have produced “no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities” and that it adheres to “all applicable export control regulations.”

It is not clear exactly what role Alice Huang currently plays at Megaspeed. The Singaporean company did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Foreign Policy, but it said in a statement to the New York Times that it took the allegations around her actions “extremely seriously” and would “conduct a thorough internal investigation.”

Megaspeed’s website continues to list it as a key Nvidia partner, and Jensen Huang told Bloomberg in an interview last month that the relationship between the two companies was “normal and not unusual.”

The Financial Times reported on Monday that Alice Huang had pitched Chinese investors touting her ability to secure advanced Nvidia technology.

Tech billionaires spent big, and data centers became a lightning rod.

Fixating on low-likelihood, high-impact scenarios misses the forest for the trees.

Trump’s latest proposal would cede the United States’ AI advantage.

China has consistently denied spying on Jensen Huang, with Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun slamming the allegations as “purely unsubstantiated and directed at smearing China” in a briefing on Monday.

Trump—who was reportedly briefed on the intelligence on Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang a year ago but did not act on it—is standing by the tech executive for the moment, telling reporters on Monday that Huang was a “very high-quality person” and an “amazing guy” who was “suffering greatly.” The U.S. president did not reveal when he first learned about the scandal, only saying it was “not too long ago.” Trump added that he had spoken to Huang earlier on Monday. “He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy, … and I really believe him,” Trump said.

Last December, Huang successfully petitioned the Trump administration to relax some restrictions on sales of the company’s second-tier chips to China—giving the U.S. government a 25 percent cut of some sales in the process.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for additional comment from Foreign Policy on the allegations against Huang.

Nvidia’s board of directors announced the launch of its own investigation on Sunday, which it said will be conducted by a “committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel.” “While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information,” the announcement said. The company also said Huang would continue in his current role during the inquiry.

Huang said he would fully cooperate with the investigation. “I love our country and our company,” he wrote in his statement. “I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American.”

But the market is already reacting. Nvidia stock dropped more than 5 percent on Monday and has plunged by more than 15 percent in the past week.

U.S. lawmakers also want answers. Republican Reps. Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford—who chair the House committees on foreign affairs, the Chinese Communist Party, and intelligence, respectively—sent a letter to Huang and Nvidia last week requesting that he testify in front of their committees on Nov. 18, giving him a deadline of Wednesday to respond.

The scandal is likely to cast a shadow over Trump’s upcoming meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, next week—the third time this year that the two leaders will be meeting. Huang attended both of the previous meetings in Beijing and Washington as one of several U.S. tech CEOs whom Trump invited to join. Trump said he had no plans to bring up Huang’s case during next week’s trip but added, “I’m sure President Xi will ask me about it.”

Trump’s embrace of Huang is likely to have its limits despite the public show of support thus far, said a former senior U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity.

“I think it’s going to be much more difficult for [Trump] to embrace Jensen Huang politically or commercially in the midst of a major investigation that will be bipartisan on what happened, who knew, what was done about it,” said the official. “My guess is that the president may not say that he’s distanced himself, but I think Jensen will find that every time … he wants to meet with the president, it will be inconvenient on scheduling.”

Asked on Sunday whether Huang would join Trump on his trip to Shenzhen, the president said: “I don’t know, but I’d certainly take him.”

Update, Nov. 9, 2026: This article has been updated to add new remarks from U.S. President Donald Trump.

#5992. Thune will lead Republicans through the minority

Senate Majority Leader John Thune was reelected as the Republican leader on Tuesday and will steer the conference through their time in the minority.

The South Dakotan ran uncontested despite a push from some of his colleagues to delay the leadership elections following Republicans’ stunning defeats last week in the midterms, which saw them lose at least seven seats and the majority.

“Obviously, the election result was not what we hoped for,” Thune told reporters, referring to the midterms. “But I think it’s important that we take the lessons from that and internalize the message the American people were sending to us.”

While he and the rest of the leadership slate sailed through the conference contests by voice vote, it wasn’t without drama.

Before the leadership elections began in the Old Supreme Court Chamber early Tuesday morning, the conference held a meeting at the request of a group of GOP five senators, led by Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis.

The conversation, which several senators described as “frank,” ended up pushing back the leadership elections by a few hours. But they were not postponed to another day as some had hoped.

“This has never been anything against John Thune,” said Johnson, as he made good on his commitment to leave the room early if the conference proceeded with its election. “What I didn’t agree with was holding the election right away, giving nobody an opportunity to really challenge any leadership position.”

“Part of the issue here is who wants the job? God bless him for serving,” Johnson added.

The conference conversation Tuesday morning turned into an “open-mic” with both conservatives and those who lost their elections speaking, according to senators.

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., told reporters, “To rush into this and to just ratify all the same leadership — I mean, what message does that send?”

But no contender to Thune emerged despite the angst, and a motion to proceed to the election, introduced by Thune’s fellow South Dakotan Sen. Mike Rounds, was accepted.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said voters who rejected Republicans last week were reacting to high gas prices, the war in Iran and the cost of living, not to how Senate leaders were running the conference.

“I don’t think anybody in Texas who voted for the Democrat governor was voting against John Thune. If you diagnose that as a problem, you’re misdiagnosing the problem,” Paul said.

Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo., was reelected to his position, as was the chairman of the Senate Republican Conference, Tom Cotton of Arkansas. Sen. James Lankford of Oklahoma was again selected as vice chair of the conference, while Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia was reelected as Republican Policy Committee chair.

“Our first step is to make sure the American people know that we heard what they said, and the American people’s priorities are our priorities. That’s the way we regain their trust,” Barrasso said afterward.

Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio got the nod to chair the National Republican Senatorial Committee, meaning he will helm the campaign arm as the party looks ahead to the uncertain waters of 2028.

Moreno said, “I was in the retail automobile business, so when you don’t listen to your customers, your customers punish you. I think we have to own it, and I think we have to learn from it.”

Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., said on Monday evening, “What we as a conference right now need is honesty. We need focus. We need to try to reach a consensus on what we need to change.”

Kennedy was among those pushing to delay the leadership elections and told reporters on Tuesday he voted present instead of yes on whether to proceed to them.

Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., who ran for GOP leader twice — once in 2022 against Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., and in 2024 against Thune — declined to run again to challenge Thune. But in a Dear Colleague letter on Monday, he detailed what he’d like to see in the lame-duck session before Democrats take power, including confirming every nominee President Donald Trump has sent to the Senate, funding the government without an omnibus, banning stock trading, passing the permitting bill that is advancing this week in the Senate, passing the National Defense Authorization Act, balancing the budget and pushing through a sweeping voter ID bill known as the SAVE America Act.

Senate Republicans on Tuesday also voted on a resolution on their path forward that was spurred by a motion from Scott, aides said.

“It is the sense of the GOP Conference that we will maximize the 54 days we have with congressional majorities, to confirm every judicial nominee and every executive nominee that the conference approves of, to pass our core Republican priorities, and to do everything humanly possible to pass a reconciliation bill before Jan. 3,” the resolution reads in part.

That long list of goals highlights the expectations Thune has faced as leader, where he led one-third of Republicans’ trifecta in Washington. In the next Congress, Democrats will hold the majority in both chambers of Congress after their larger-than-expected wins, while Trump finishes out his term as president.

Thune said he told his conference: “As I look back on the last couple of years, my question is, what would you have me do differently?”

“Given the constraints we had to deal with, all the stuff that was coming at us on a daily basis, a narrow margin in the House, the White House, the Democrats over here who were obstructing two long government shutdowns — I think we came out of it as well as could have been expected, and got a lot of stuff done,” Thune told reporters.

“If you believe the exit polls, it was the war, it was the economy, it was inflation, it was fuel prices,” Thune added. “So no, I wasn’t apologizing for anything that we did. And I think on the political side, I don’t know what else I could have done.”

#5991. North Korea’s Enemies Within

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

How Long Will Elites Stay Loyal to Kim Jong Un?

In 2015, the North Korean diplomat Thae Yong Ho received an unusual assignment. Kim Jong Chol, the older brother of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, was coming to London to attend an Eric Clapton concert, and Thae, who was then stationed in London, was assigned to look after him. Providing direct service to the ruling family confers honor on North Korean officials and their households, so Thae expected his two sons to be impressed.

To Thae’s surprise, his sons were outraged. Ordinary North Koreans could be expelled from university (or worse) for listening to Western music, they told him. And now the Kim family was spending thousands of dollars in a single evening to enjoy entertainment forbidden to all other North Koreans. In the eyes of his children, Thae later wrote in his memoir, Password to the Third Floor, he was a prisoner forced to take care of a prison warden. Their reaction left him ashamed.

The next year, Thae, his wife, and their sons escaped to South Korea. His defection surprised the international community. Only weeks earlier, Thae had been defending the North Korean regime with great fervor. Yet this incongruous behavior is familiar to those who understand life among North Korea’s elite: officials can profess full devotion to the Kim family right until the day they run.

The gap between public conduct and private belief is difficult to observe from the outside. For over a decade, I interviewed dozens of former diplomats, Korean Workers’ Party cadres, military officers, businesspeople, and technicians, all of whom had lived, studied, or worked in Pyongyang. These people ran the party, military, embassies, foreign-currency businesses, and technical programs on which the state depends for its survival. They received the best education, housing, food, and access to influential social networks their country could provide. Some once believed sincerely in the system; others learned early that loyalty was a role they had to pantomime in a nationwide, lifelong performance—now with Kim Jong Un as the maestro. Nearly all described an elite class under growing strain.

Since Kim Jong Un came to power in December 2011, he has tightened his grip on the country’s elites by carrying out sweeping purges of the old guard of senior party officials and military officers and executing others for minor political missteps. Many members of North Korea’s elite fear that they or their families can be killed at the drop of a hat. And their escape routes are narrowing; since Kim sealed off the borders during the COVID-19 pandemic, the number of North Korean defectors reaching South Korea has plummeted.

Those North Koreans who still manage to escape increasingly come from the elite. As of August 2024, South Korea’s National Intelligence Service reported that the number of defections from North Korea’s upper class recorded under Kim Jong Un was two and a half times the combined total observed during the reigns of Kim Il Sung (1948 to 1994) and Kim Jong Il (1994 to 2011). The absolute number remains small—in the hundreds—and it would be a mistake to interpret this trend as a harbinger of imminent regime collapse. North Korea is remarkably effective at preventing private grievances from becoming organized opposition. The regime does not need every official to believe in it. But it needs its doubters to feel isolated and alone in their skepticism and disillusionment.

North Korea has long been referred to as the “Hermit Kingdom,” but that term offers the wrong impression of the country. It is not totally isolated from the world. It is a nuclear-armed state with diplomatic relations with over 160 countries, and it has the world’s fourth-largest standing army and highly skilled cyber-operators. The vast majority of the population may be fed a robust diet of state propaganda, but most elites are exposed to life outside North Korea. They have a reasonable sense of how the world works and their country’s place in it. And yet they have to live with intense cognitive dissonance, at once understanding the real world and having to create, enforce, and trumpet the state’s official narratives to their countrymen and foreigners.

Many high-ranking North Koreans are finding it harder to sustain this balancing act. Access to privilege can purchase compliance—and terror can enforce it—but the state will not give elites what they increasingly want: guaranteed security for them and their families and a viable future for their children. Kim can allay some frustrations by doling out luxury apartments, promotions, and access to extravagant lifestyles. He cannot address the deeper sources of discontent without relaxing the very controls that protect his family’s rule from challenges to its power. The regime remains capable of suppressing any organized resistance in the country, but the growing disaffection of the elite threatens to weaken the state from within. Kim presides over a system increasingly marked by doubt, suspicion, and pervasive anxiety. When the chips are down and North Korea faces a true crisis, its most powerful leaders may not know who they can trust and where they can turn.

Most of the more than 34,000 North Koreans now living in South Korea came from the poor northern provinces along the Chinese border. Many of them fled to the south to escape famine and economic hardship. They had little access to the regime’s inner workings, even if they had tremendous experience of its cruelty and depredations. In contrast, elite escapees come from a wholly different world. They are products of Pyongyang, a capital of roughly three million that is closed to most of the country’s 25 million citizens. They grew up with relatively reliable electricity and running water, and attended schools designed to educate the next generation of regime operators. They benefited from the new construction of luxury residential districts, extravagant resort towns such as Samjiyon and Wonsan-Kalma, and the country’s sustained economic growth in the face of heavy international sanctions. North Korea’s elite serve in a range of occupations beyond just the party cadre ranks, the military, and the security services; they can be artists, software engineers, restaurant managers, and much else. The regime groomed them from birth to serve the party and the Kim family.

Consider the family of Ri Jong Ho and his son Hyunseung Lee. Ri spent three decades in Office 39, which earns and manages foreign currency for the leadership. Kim Jong Il appointed him to senior trade and economic posts, and in 2002 the state awarded him a Hero of Labor medal and a Kim Il Sung watch, prestigious honors and a recognition of his loyalty and patriotism. Ri’s son attended some of the country’s finest educational institutions, including Kumsong Academy and Pyongyang Foreign Language Institute, which prepare the children of senior cadres to enter high positions in the party. Hyunseung and his sister were also among the rare few North Koreans who were permitted to study abroad in China. By his mid-20s, Hyunseung was already a party member, working in China, and was trusted to chair a branch of the Kim Il Sung Youth League while helping facilitate millions of dollars in trade between Chinese companies and North Korea. This family faithfully served their country while living at the highest echelons of their society and enjoying the best creature comforts. But their privileged positions did not make them safe.

The shocking 2013 execution of Jang Song Thaek, Kim Jong Un’s uncle, unnerved Ri. The slain Jang had been married to Kim Il Sung’s daughter and had served all three Kims. If the regime could eliminate such a decorated official—and a member of the ruling family—and seek to erase him from the country’s history and memory, then no one was untouchable. Ri’s family escaped to South Korea from their posts in China in 2014, and Hyunseung and his sister later earned master’s degrees from Columbia University. Despite the many privileges their family received from the regime, they fled because their proximity to power made them feel deeply vulnerable.

North Koreans live under institutions designed to make independent organization impossible. Party committees operate inside every school, embassy, farm, military unit, office, and factory. Security bureaus obsessively police information flows and political conduct, while neighborhood units monitor every household. Every citizen, starting at a young age, belongs to a state-directed organization. For elites, closeness to power invites suffocating scrutiny; it places them more deeply within the grasp of the state rather than freeing them from the overbearing system.

The Organization and Guidance Department, the party’s most powerful agency, oversees appointments, inspections, and discipline everywhere—in Pyongyang as well as rural villages. No escapee is known to have come from the OGD’s central ranks, an indication of the control imposed on the country’s most influential officials. Diplomats and workers sent abroad must surrender their passports and leave relatives in North Korea as collateral to deter defection. When they come home, they must account for what they saw, heard, and did abroad, enumerate every single political sin they committed, and then undergo extensive ideological deprogramming and reprogramming.

Kim Se Yun (a pseudonym), a former senior party cadre who traveled overseas, described the monthlong central review she underwent every time she returned to Pyongyang. Officials have to “cleanse” themselves of what they have encountered and report even small details, including whether they had gone out drinking with colleagues after dinner. A late night out could require a written piece of self-flagellation to account for a lapse unbecoming of “a devoted worker for the state.” The review was meant to minimize the effects of foreign exposure: a person could see how others lived but, upon returning, had to renounce what she had seen. Kim Se Yun described the constant surveillance when abroad and at home as miserable and utterly asphyxiating.

An elite position brings goods, status, and influence denied to ordinary citizens, but it also places a person’s career, relatives, and life within reach of the leader who can destroy them at any point for any reason. As one common saying in Pyongyang has it, “The closer you are to the sun, the more likely you will burn.”

Nothing impressed this lesson upon the elite class more forcefully than the fall of Jang in 2013. His sudden arrest and execution sent lasting fear through Pyongyang. Every elite I spoke with understood the warning implicit in his killing.

Jang had already undergone “revolutionization” three times. This distinctly North Korean punishment, used especially to discipline and defenestrate high officials, strips a person of office and sends him to perform physical labor and political reeducation, often in the countryside. It humiliates an elite official in front of the people he once commanded, even if it does not foreclose the possibility of his future rehabilitation. Jang returned each time, only to be executed in the end by the third leader he served. Heo Kang Il, an elite defector who managed a North Korean restaurant in China and in 2016 brought 12 of his staff with him to South Korea, knew people subjected to revolutionization and was subjected to it once himself. He told me that many never recovered even after being rehabilitated. Some developed psychological illnesses or died within a few years from physical ailments.

When Kim Jong Un became the country’s leader in December 2011, he was in his late 20s (his exact birth year is unknown). He aggressively imposed his writ by carrying out purges of party senior cadres and military officials who had served under his two predecessors. Outside observers described his vicious consolidation of power as an attempt to compensate for his youth, his limited political experience, and his complete lack of a military background. When the COVID-19 pandemic hit, Kim Jong Un reinforced the country’s already hard borders to eliminate any unauthorized cross-border movement and passed draconian laws that further criminalized consumption of any unauthorized foreign media, all with the aim of “repurifying” the country’s socialist Korean culture. Although the pandemic has passed, the information environment is more controlled than ever before and the borders remain sealed.

In North Korea, loyalty is evaluated and documented from childhood. A person’s conduct at school; performance in political organizations; and songbun status (a hereditary classification of loyalty to the regime that breaks up North Koreans into three broad groups: “core,” “wavering,” and “hostile”), determine admission to universities, party membership, and promotion. Adults attend regular self-criticism sessions. At home, portraits of the Kims must hang spotless at the highest point of the most prominent wall, with nothing placed above them. One woman I interviewed recalled habitation inspectors making regular visits in white gloves to check the portraits for dust. She cleaned the portraits meticulously, not because she revered the men in them but because a speck of dust could endanger her family.

Even a weekly public self-criticism session, which requires a person to publicly share a political transgression they have made and then criticize a colleague, often becomes a coordinated performance. Many elite defectors told me that the day before a self-criticism session, colleagues would warn one another about what they planned to criticize at the next day’s session. The advance notice protected friendships while allowing everyone to satisfy the requirements of the political cleansing ritual. A person might confess to lacking sufficient revolutionary zeal during the previous week and vehemently rebuke a friend for a similar offense. The trick was to disclose transgressions that were sufficiently blameworthy but not serious enough to get oneself or a colleague in too much trouble.

Another former elite described the public mourning after Kim Jong Il’s death in 2011. She felt relief at the leader’s death, and no sorrow, but knew that she had to appear to cry, so she dredged up her saddest memories—those of her grandmother’s death and of a cousin who was forcibly repatriated after a failed defection—to force herself to weep. When tears still would not come, she bowed her head, dramatically shook her shoulders, and avoided eye contact with anyone in the hysterically wailing crowd. She believed that many people around her were giving the same performance.

Scholars refer to this gap as preference falsification: people publicly misrepresent their true beliefs because honesty is dangerous. In Pyongyang, preference falsification is an essential part of ordinary daily life. Elites constantly calibrate their speech and compartmentalize their innermost private thoughts. Some still believe in the system or feel genuine national pride. Others resent Kim while valuing the status his regime gives them. Belief and cynicism can exist in the same office and within the same person. This is how a senior diplomat can lecture British bureaucrats about North Korea’s victimhood one day and then flee North Korea with his entire family a few weeks later.

When elites do leave, their departures remind others who harbor private doubts that they are not alone. This is one reason Pyongyang treats prominent defections as security emergencies. When Heo (the restaurant manager) and 12 workers left a North Korean restaurant in China in 2016, the state recalled all other workers in China for interrogation. In his memoir, Thae analogized this group defection to stones falling from a castle wall: small losses can eventually lead to the collapse of the entire castle.

Nobody lightly gives up their lofty place in the pecking order of North Korean society. Kim Jong Un has not neglected his ruling class. His government has built gleaming new housing in Pyongyang for scientists, party cadres, and other favored groups, and it distributes foreign cars, watches, jewelry, food, and apartments. An elite position also provides something less tangible: a strong sense of purpose and relevance. A bureaucrat, as powerless as he may be, matters in North Korean society. People appreciate his official title, defer to his family, and recognize the heft of his social and political connections.

The prospect of losing that status can make the thought of escape unpalatable even for people who detest the regime. Over dinner at a Seoul barbecue restaurant buzzing with customers eating sizzling meat and drinking somaek, a mixture of beer and soju, a former official I call Mr. Kim recalled an incident elsewhere in which he had asked a table of loud college students to quiet down. Decades younger than him, they barely looked at him—they “didn’t even put their drinks down.” One student told him to eat somewhere else. As he recalled the humiliation, Mr. Kim removed his glasses and rubbed his eyes. In North Korea, he told me, a restaurant would have gone silent when he entered. He would have walked with his shoulders straight and head held high, knowing that his family name and job carried weight. In South Korea, where he worked a warehouse job, he was “just a mere North Korean defector with a suspicious accent.”

Mr. Kim’s experience of losing status and purpose after defection helps explain why the regime’s mixture of privilege and coercion still works. Elites know they have a lot to risk and lose, so for most aggrieved elites, the rational option is to remain in the system, perform loyalty for the rest of their lives, and extract all the advantages their positions still offer.

Yet this bargain has an expiration date. After retirement, senior officers and cadres do not receive pensions. The government takes back state-provided cars, homes, and appliances. After serving the state for decades, retired generals and senior cadres are often reduced to working as guards or market vendors. Younger elites watch this happen and accumulate money as much as possible, knowing that the state that demands their whole lives will not care for them in their old age.

Younger and middle-aged elites are also less inclined to put up with the careers and sacrifices the state has historically presented as honorable. Many interviewees told me that elite parents no longer want their sons to spend over a decade conscripted in the army or build careers entirely inside the party. They prefer business, technical work, study abroad, and amassing private wealth. They want access to the outside world and would welcome greater economic liberalization at home, even if they do not expect full democracy or the reunification of the peninsula in the near future. Above all, they want their children to have lives less constrained than their own.

Money has altered the old order in what Kim Jong Un calls a “socialist paradise.” During one interview, an escapee told me that he knew who would succeed Kim Jong Un to become North Korea’s fourth ruler. I expected him to name Kim Jong Un’s daughter or sister. “Money,” he said. He was being cheeky, but only partly. He pulled out his phone and read the biblical warning that no one can serve two masters, God and money; in his analogy, Kim occupied the place of God. North Koreans jostle for food, better education, and influence, and search for ways to make money outside state-sanctioned activities by paying bribes and using black markets. Younger elites increasingly judge a good marriage, job, and future career path in terms of how it can offer them access to cash and useful business connections. A title remains useful, often because it can be converted into income. The collapse of the state’s public distribution system and devastating famine years of the 1990s drove the grassroot marketization of the country, with the development of state-regulated marketplaces, some so large that they’ve hosted over 10,000 vendors. Presently, in this de jure socialist country that officially condemns capitalism, markets and the imperative of earning hard cash shape people’s daily lives.

This change appears in ordinary choices. One former businessman carried a two-dollar bill in his wallet as a good-luck charm to attract prosperity and wealth. Other interviewees remembered a time when families seeking husbands for their daughters preferred sons of party cadres; today, a man with access to foreign currency or a profitable business can be much more desirable. Political rank still opens doors, but money can keep them open.

Kim has accommodated some of these economic changes; once prohibited, markets are now regulated and taxed by the state. Although foreign media and the Internet remain strictly prohibited, the state allows North Koreans to access a highly controlled intranet and use smartphones with local software and applications. It grants apartments to selected families and permits officials to enrich themselves by engaging in business ventures, provided they continue to perform their jobs exquisitely and contribute mandatory “loyalty funds” to the state.

What Kim cannot offer is dependable and lasting safety. Everything remains subordinate to the leader’s needs and whims. An official who follows the law may still be punished for crossing a better-connected family, and a successful cadre may be swept away because his patron was purged.

Growing elite grievances do not mean an uprising is near. A disaffected elite has five options: remain silent and maintain the status quo; flee the country; build parallel networks of money and influence; protest; or push for incremental reform. The last three are extraordinarily dangerous in North Korea. The regime will extinguish dissent, bids for reform, and any networks that strive to operate or even seem to operate beyond the state’s control. For most, the choice then narrows to either carrying one’s grievances to the grave or mustering the courage and resolve to defect.

Most people opt to stay. Through imposing guilt by association and collective punishments, the North Korean state has spent decades attenuating the relationships through which private anger might be converted into collective action. Its surveillance system encourages colleagues, neighbors, and even relatives to watch and report one another. Unapproved associations and even impromptu sports matches at schools that bring together more than a few people are forbidden unless they are specially approved, and the state tightly controls information about purges and acts of protest to prevent the spread of dissension. In some border cities, such as Sinuiju, the party has recently banned any unapproved gatherings of three or more people.

When I discussed the obstacles to collective action with Lee Chul Eun, a former high-ranking official in the Ministry of State Security who defected in 2016 by swimming six kilometers to South Korea, he described the state’s security apparatus as a spiderweb of security agents, surveillance offices, military commands, and party bodies. A person would have to be “absolutely insane” to challenge such a system, he told me. Another former official summarized the social knowledge produced by that web: “We [elites] know everything but just don’t express it.” Elites can recognize propaganda, corruption, and private anger around them while not knowing whom they can fully trust to confide in.

The regime has other sources of durability. Trade with China, weapons sales, cybertheft from foreign banks and companies, and sending North Korean laborers abroad all help fund the regime’s operations, including its nuclear weapons program, security services, national network of political prison camps, and luxuries necessary for managing elites. The regime has survived famine, international sanctions, and leadership successions. Discontent has been building for years without ever transforming into any form of sustained, organized opposition.

This helps explain another surprising finding from my interviews and research. Many elites understand that the official story is false. They know that colleagues complain in private, seek bribes, watch foreign media, and concoct safe ways for their children to remain and work abroad. What they cannot safely determine is who would follow and stand with them if they tried to protest and push for reform. First movers are the most vulnerable to state repression, while everyone else can deny sharing the same views. North Korea’s political system depends on atomization and making doubters feel isolated from one another. The regime understands that the most plausible organized threat to its hold on the state would be Pyongyang powered, not people powered; a challenge or rebellion is more likely to start among elite insiders than as a mass revolt from below. But for now, elites don’t trust one another and lack the shared vision required to move against the regime.

Defection is the one option an individual can choose without first building a coalition. Elite escapees take with them expertise and signal to peers that leaving is possible. Yet China continues to forcibly repatriate North Koreans who cross its border. Officials posted abroad wishing to defect must dexterously evade state security officials stationed alongside them and come to peace with the fact that loved ones back home will surely be punished.

In August 2025, a North Korean interpreter traveling with a delegation from Pyongyang’s Academy of Social Sciences entered the South Korean embassy in Ulaanbaatar in Mongolia and asked to defect. A year later, the request is still unresolved and the interpreter remains in limbo in the embassy. Mongolia, which maintains relations with Pyongyang, has been slow to cooperate. North Korea objected, and Seoul, currently under a left-leaning administration that seeks warmer relations with the North, will not even confirm that the case existed. For officials considering escape, the lesson is stark: even reaching the embassy of an ostensibly democratic country may not deliver them from the tyranny of home.

Several elite defectors I spoke with had reached the United States and applied for asylum. Their claims have languished for years or been rejected; one claimant has waited more than nine years. They cycle through hearings and background checks with no resolution to their cases. A former North Korean official could certainly pose a counterintelligence risk. But keeping them in this purgatory tells others that the United States may be happy to take their valuable intelligence while still not offering them a future. The vagaries of American asylum policy are not responsible for the persistence of the Kim family regime, but Washington’s reluctance to welcome these defectors could suggest to wavering elites in Pyongyang that it might just be safer to stay put.

Kim Jong Un can continue to manage elite disaffection by rotating, purging, rewarding, and surveilling the very people who keep his regime running on a daily basis. But this approach provides only symptomatic relief to the overarching and insoluble crisis produced by his totalitarianism. To gain the confidence of his elites, he would have to stop using purges and executions, end the collective punishment of families for the transgressions of an individual, close political prison camps, permit freer flows of information, and allow for autonomous market activity without the fear of unpredictable shutdowns and confiscations. Each concession, however, reduces the fear and isolation of elites. To Kim’s detriment, that would only embolden elites to turn against him.

He will likely not relax his grip on the ranks of the powerful. But in so doing, he will weaken his own regime. The costs of preference falsification and performative loyalty will accumulate among the highest echelons of the regime’s operators. That will become most dangerous during a succession struggle or severe economic shock. In ordinary times, each official can continue assuming that all his colleagues will strive to maintain the status quo. But a crisis—such as a military coup, another volcanic eruption of Mount Paektu, or an economic meltdown—can change those assumptions swiftly.

In a moment of upheaval and uncertainty, already disaffected officials may conclude that obedient compliance will no longer protect their positions or their families. Officials who appear loyal today might withhold cooperation from a startled regime, engage in a power struggle, or defect en masse. If enough regime operators make these calculations, then Kim will find that the people he depends on to carry out his orders are prioritizing their own survival over that of his regime. And he could lose his hold on the country.

My interviews with erstwhile members of North Korea’s elite do not point to imminent regime collapse. Rather, they suggest a more haunting vulnerability for the Kim family: the loyalty of the elites, which is critical for regime survival, is becoming more performative, less genuine, and motivated by self-preservation, not a wellspring of ideological conviction. The regime’s habitual recourse to maximalist punishments and mass purges will likely drive more elites to defect and maybe, more strikingly, muster unprecedented expressions of collective action. Kim will face his last days when a large enough body of North Korean elites conclude that remaining loyal is no longer their safest and most rational choice.

JIEUN BAEK is the author of Privileged but Powerless: How North Korean Elite Grievances Reveal the Regime’s Greatest Weakness, from which this essay is adapted, and North Korea’s Hidden Revolution: How the Information Underground Is Transforming a Closed Society.

U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s name wasn’t on the ballot in last week’s midterms, but he still may end up being one of their biggest losers.

Top Republicans, including U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance, have blamed the Iran war for their midterms wipeout. With Hegseth having played a key role prosecuting and cheerleading the war, he’s a prime target for intraparty retribution post-midterms.

U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s name wasn’t on the ballot in last week’s midterms, but he still may end up being one of their biggest losers.

Top Republicans, including U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance, have blamed the Iran war for their midterms wipeout. With Hegseth having played a key role prosecuting and cheerleading the war, he’s a prime target for intraparty retribution post-midterms.

Outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie, who is among U.S. President Donald Trump’s biggest Republican critics on Capitol Hill, on Monday introduced a resolution to impeach Hegseth for “high crimes and misdemeanors.” In remarks on the House floor, Massie said that the defense secretary “knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders to initiate war against a foreign nation.” He also said that Hegseth has demonstrated that he will remain a “threat” to the U.S. Constitution.

Massie’s resolution contains eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth, accusing him of waging the Iran war without congressional authorization and ignoring laws that minimize civilian casualties. Other articles focus on lethal U.S. strikes on alleged drug boats near Latin America, which Massie described as “extrajudicial killings,” and the U.S. operation to capture former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. The resolution characterized the Maduro raid as the unlawful “kidnapping of a sovereign foreign leader.”

Massie previously introduced impeachment articles against Hegseth in September, but House Speaker Mike Johnson blocked the effort—pushing it until after the midterms—by recessing the lower chamber early. The House now has until Wednesday to schedule a vote.

The chances of the articles passing are “far more likely now than before the election,” Massie told CNN on Monday. Impeaching Hegseth requires a simple majority vote in the House. However, Johnson urged lawmakers against impeaching Hegseth, stating that it would be a “terrible look” while the country is in the “middle of hostilities abroad.”

Meanwhile, top House Democrats are also lining up behind the effort to impeach Hegseth. Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is poised to be the next House speaker, told ABC News on Sunday that he’s a “hard yes” on the impeachment resolution and that he believes there will be “incredibly strong support” among the rest of House Democrats.

It’s harder to say whether there would be enough support in the GOP-controlled Senate to reach the two-thirds supermajority vote necessary to convict and remove Hegseth. It’s also an open question if there’s enough time in the current congressional session for there to be an impeachment trial in the Senate. But Democrats could also push to impeach Hegseth again in a new Congress.

Even if Hegseth survives impeachment and Trump continues to back him, the defense secretary is poised to face relentless scrutiny after Democrats assume control of Congress on Jan. 3. Democrats have made it clear that they plan to fully leverage their oversight powers—and that Hegseth will be in their crosshairs. This means investigations, hearings, and subpoenas are coming. Democrats have already indicated that they want more answers from Hegseth on everything from the Iran war to the boat strikes.

Rep. Adam Smith, the ranking member on the House Armed Services Committee, vowed to conduct “vigorous oversight” of the U.S. Defense Department in a new Congress. “The list of potential oversight topics is long, but the illegal war against Iran is top of mind for me and the American people,” he said.

But as the walls close in around him, Hegseth has remained defiant.

In comments to reporters on Monday before Massie introduced the articles of impeachment, Hegseth made no apologies. “If you want to take issue with what we did in Epic Fury, or Rough Rider, or nabbing Nicolás Maduro, you’re taking issue with the troops and what they accomplished,” he said. (Operation Epic Fury is the U.S. military’s name for the first phase of the Iran war, from February to May, while Operation Rough Rider is the Pentagon’s name for the U.S. military campaign against the Houthis in Yemen last spring.)

Last week, Hegseth released a video taking aim at his political opponents. “This is not about me, but of course the other side, they’re obsessed. A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democratic allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly. Just like they tried against President Trump twice,” he said.

The video landed poorly even among some Republicans. “@PeteHegseth, cabinet secretaries shouldn’t be wasting taxpayer dollars on campaign style videos. Kristi Noem learned that the hard way,” Sen. Thom Tillis posted on X. “This is about you,” he added, accusing Hegseth of displaying incompetence, offering bad advice to Trump, and being involved in “shameful” and embarrassing “episodes from firing our top generals to texting war plans to reporters.” Tillis was seemingly referring to the Signalgate controversy—a major national security scandal that Hegseth was at the center of early last year.

In many ways, it comes as no surprise that Hegseth is now in the crosshairs of Democrats and Republicans alike. He’s been a combative and divisive Pentagon chief from the start, spending much of his energy waging culture wars—such as by moving to ban transgender people from serving in the military and targeting diversity, equity, and inclusion policies—while using the Defense Department as a platform to promote his far-right Christian views. He’s also ruffled feathers by pushing out top military leaders and denying promotions for Black and women soldiers. Meanwhile, Hegseth has had an extraordinarily contentious dynamic with the press, effectively hollowing out the Pentagon press corps after major outlets refused to agree to restrictions that he sought to impose on their reporting.

Hegseth has made a lot of enemies in Washington in the process, and he seems to have fewer allies by the day. Even months before the midterms, there were signs that some Republican lawmakers were souring on him. As Republicans play the blame game over their losses in the midterms, support for Hegseth appears to be cratering—even among GOP lawmakers who are wary of publicly supporting impeachment.

When asked about where he stands on impeaching Hegseth, Rep. James Comer, the chair of the House Oversight Committee, told NewsNation: “I can tell you with a high level of confidence that there’s a lot of questions about Hegseth. We have no idea what the strategy is moving forward in Iran. No one’s happy about Iran, and I think the Republican voters are more upset about what’s going on in Iran than the Democrat voters.”

On Monday, Rep. Don Bacon told reporters that he was weighing whether to support Massie’s impeachment resolution. But he also said that it would be better for Hegseth to resign. “I don’t think he was the right choice to begin with,” he said.

Trump has so far stood by Hegseth and pushed back against questions about the defense secretary’s job security. “He’s guilty of two things, basically winning two wars,” Trump said of Hegseth on Sunday. “I believe we saved the Middle East and Israel combined. And it’s awfully hard to say ‘let’s impeach’ somebody who did that.”

Hegseth has been among Trump’s most loyal cabinet secretaries since he returned to the White House, and critics have portrayed Hegseth as a prime example of the yes-men culture surrounding Trump. But loyalty hasn’t always paid off for those in the president’s orbit, as he has a history of turning on even his most faithful advisors. Recent reports suggest that Trump has been asking allies about a potential replacement for Hegseth. Trump has also acknowledged receiving calls from people who are unhappy with the Pentagon chief, though he said that he didn’t understand why.
